ADJ-04.title: Weighted conformal prediction keeps its marginal guarantee under shift by returning infinite intervals where the source has no data
ADJ-04.question: Does weighted conformal prediction give valid intervals for target patients under covariate shift, including where the source has no data?
ADJ-04.answer: No. Weighted conformal intervals kept marginal coverage over the target (0.904 to 0.919 at nominal 0.9), but beyond the source's largest covariate value they covered 0.70 at a small shift and 0.83 at a moderate one, and at the largest shift they covered 0.99 only because 83% of those intervals were infinite. The method makes the support problem visible; it does not solve it. Estimating the density ratio changed nothing.
findings: Beyond the source's range: split conformal 0.63 to 0.68; weighted 0.70, 0.83, 0.99 at target means 0.5, 1, 1.5.
Infinite intervals beyond the range: 0%, 11% and 83% at the three shifts (true ratio); 0%, 14% and 82% with the estimated ratio.
Calibration ESS matched n exp(-mu^2) at mu 0.5 and 1 and exceeded it at 1.5 (51 against 32).
ADJ-04.not_answered: Prediction intervals for individual outcomes rather than a marginal treatment effect; one covariate and one outcome model; no BART or Gaussian process arm; no support diagnostic scored as a classifier. Peer review has not been done.
ADJ-04.design: Spline outcome model with curvature where the source is thin; ordinary, true-ratio weighted and estimated-ratio weighted split conformal intervals at three target shifts; coverage overall and beyond the source's range, infinite intervals and calibration effective sample size. 3 cells, 500 replicates each.
ADJ-04.estimand: Coverage of 90% prediction intervals for target patients' outcomes, overall and beyond the source's covariate range
methods_compared: weighted conformal with the true density ratio
weighted conformal with a logistic-regression density ratio

ADJ-09.title: An invariance screen for a bridging assumption, scored as a classifier
ADJ-09.question: Does instability across observed trials predict failure of a bridge used in a gap with no data, and does a screen on marginal effects fire under a valid bridge through non-collapsibility?
ADJ-09.answer: A stability screen across observed trials cannot confirm a bridge and refutes it rarely. With 4 or 10 trials, drift visible across them that biased the gap estimate by 0.28 was flagged in only 20% to 24% of analyses, and drift confined to the gap never above the null rate; passing the screen did not improve coverage of the reported analyses. Screening marginal log odds ratios raised false abstention under a valid bridge from 0.11 to 0.19 to 0.24 through non-collapsibility; screening conditional or standardized effects removed that.
findings: Primary confirmed: under a valid bridge with strong prognosis, marginal minus conditional abstention 0.077 (SE 0.016) with 4 trials and 0.113 (SE 0.017) with 10; standardized within 0.03 of conditional.
Visible drift of 0.15 per unit (gap bias about 0.28): abstention 0.20 to 0.24; of 0.3 per unit (gap bias about 0.56): 0.50 to 0.67.
Gap-only drift: abstention within Monte Carlo error of the valid-bridge rate while the gap estimate was biased by up to 0.60.
Coverage among analyses that passed the screen differed from coverage among all analyses by at most 0.011.
Controls: identical trials 0.099 to 0.104; collapsible risk-difference model, marginal screen 0.117; large drift 0.990 or more.
ADJ-09.not_answered: One event-rate level, no measurement shift, Cochran's Q only; environments valid by construction. Peer review has not been done.
ADJ-09.design: K trials with differing covariate laws and a gap environment; Cochran's Q screen with abstention on marginal, conditional and standardized log odds ratios; valid bridge, drift visible in the trials, and drift confined to the gap; 20 cells and 3 controls, 1000 replicates each.
ADJ-09.estimand: Conditional log odds ratio in the gap environment
methods_compared: Cochran's Q screen on marginal log odds ratios
on standardized marginal log odds ratios

ADJ-10.title: Modifier discovery across trials: no penalty is both stable and powerful, and study-level heterogeneity creates a false modifier that more trials entrench
ADJ-10.question: Are effect modifiers discovered from pooled trial data stable and correct enough to use, and do study-level confounders create false modifiers that more data do not remove?
ADJ-10.answer: No. Lasso discovery at the minimum-error penalty found the true modifiers but added 1.7 to 2.8 false ones among seven null covariates, and sets from independent datasets agreed with Jaccard similarity 0.37 to 0.57; the one-standard-error rule was stable only by selecting nothing (a single modifier found in 3% to 5% of analyses). With an unmeasured study-level cause of effect heterogeneity, pooled discovery selected the covariate whose trial means tracked it in 69% of analyses with 3 trials and 93% with 12 at the same total size, and raised false discoveries among the other covariates from 1.7 to 2.8 per analysis to 3.6 to 3.9; trial-specific treatment effects removed both.
findings: Usability condition (stability at least 0.8 with at most 0.5 false modifiers in every cell) failed for every method and penalty.

Pooled minimum-error discovery selected the confounded covariate in 0.69, 0.81, 0.93 of analyses with 3, 6, 12 trials (one true modifier); within-trial discovery 0.14 to 0.46, the rate of any null covariate.
Pooled minimum-error target bias under confounding 0.023 to 0.057; one-standard-error rule biased toward no modification by 0.09 to 0.21.
ADJ-10.not_answered: Lasso only (no multi-study causal forests); continuous outcome; linear modification; one overlap level; post-selection inference for the target not studied here. Peer review has not been done.
ADJ-10.design: Three to twelve trials at a fixed total of 2400 patients, one or three true modifiers among ten candidates, study-level confounding absent or present; pooled and within-trial lasso at two penalty rules; power, false discoveries, stability and target error. 12 cells, 300 replicates each.
ADJ-10.n_sim: 300 per cell, 12 cells, two datasets per replicate
ADJ-10.estimand: Selection of true and false effect modifiers, stability of the selected set, and the target mean difference at covariate means 0.5

ADJ-15.title: Target moments released under differential privacy
ADJ-15.question: When a target trial releases covariate moments under differential privacy, how much does ignoring the added noise cost MAIC coverage at realistic arm sizes and budgets, does propagating its known variance repair it, and when do extra released moments stop paying for their share of the budget?
ADJ-15.answer: Privacy noise is not negligible at usable budgets for trial-sized targets: at epsilon 1 and 150 patients it was 8% to 60% of the estimate's variance and ignoring it cut coverage to 0.88 to 0.94; at 40 patients to 0.73. Its variance is known exactly, and adding it restored coverage in every scenario, conservatively where noise dominated. Releasing second moments pays only at larger budgets; at small ones it made MAIC infeasible in up to 87% of replicates.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: coverage ignoring the noise was as low as 0.883 at epsilon of at least 1 and targets of at least 150.

Propagating the known noise variance gave coverage of at least 0.926 in every private scenario, the minimum matching the non-private analysis's own misspecification; it reached 1.000 where noise dominated.
Releasing means and second moments with a split budget left no feasible weights in 45% to 87% of replicates at 40 to 150 patients and epsilon 0.5 to 1.
Under quadratic modification at epsilon 4 and 150 patients second moments cut RMSE from 0.229 to 0.171.
ADJ-15.not_answered: Laplace mechanism only; Gaussian mechanism, released correlations and overlap not varied. Results are conditional on feasible weights. Budget choice and governance are outside the study. Peer review has not been done.
ADJ-15.design: MAIC to Laplace-privatized target means or means and second moments, 48 cells crossing target size (40 to 500), privacy budget, released statistics and linear or quadratic effect modification; non-private, noise-ignored and noise-propagated analyses. 1000 replicates per cell.
ADJ-15.estimand: Target-population mean difference, A versus C, at the target trial's own covariate moments
methods_compared: MAIC to private moments, noise ignored
MAIC to private moments, noise variance propagated

ADJ-17.title: An encoding that reconstructs 91% of the covariates' variance dropped the effect modifier entirely
ADJ-17.question: Can a covariate encoding learned to reconstruct the covariates drop an effect modifier while reconstructing them well, and would a declared mapping or the full covariate set avoid the resulting transport bias?
ADJ-17.answer: No. With the treatment effect modified along a low-variance direction of 20 covariates, STC on five principal components reconstructed 91% of the covariate variance and lost the whole modification: bias -0.20 at a 0.5 SD target shift and -0.40 at 1 SD, coverage 0.49 and 0.02. Ten components (95% reconstructed) still lost most of it. STC on all covariates or on a declared modifier score was unbiased with nominal coverage in every cell, so reconstruction quality does not certify an encoding for transport.
findings: Low-variance modifier: bias at 2, 5, 10 components -0.20, -0.20, -0.14 (0.5 SD shift).
High-variance modifier: kept at 5 and 10 components; partly lost at 2 because the leading directions had equal variance.
All-covariate and declared-score STC: bias within 0.01, coverage 0.937 to 0.965.
ADJ-17.not_answered: Principal components only; no treatment-effect-preserving or nonlinear encoder, nonlinear heterogeneity or measurement shift; continuous outcome. Peer review has not been done.
ADJ-17.design: Twenty covariates with five strong and fifteen weak directions; the modifier on a strong or weak direction; STC on 2, 5 or 10 principal components, on all covariates, or on a declared modifier score, standardized to a shifted target. 12 cells, 1000 replicates each.
ADJ-17.estimand: Target-population mean difference, -0.5 + 0.4 times the shift along the modifier
methods_compared: STC on a declared modifier score

CMP-03.title: An omitted component interaction biases never-administered regimens and leaks into regimens that do not contain it
CMP-03.question: When additivity makes a never-administered combination estimable, how far can an omitted component interaction move its predicted effect, and does it contaminate other regimens?
CMP-03.answer: No. At a synergy of 0.2 (twice a contrast's SE), 15 of 32 never-administered regimen results that the additive model reported as estimable had 95% coverage below 0.90, down to 0.11. Synergy on a never co-administered pair went wholly into the regimens containing it and was undetectable; synergy on a co-administered pair was absorbed into the component effects and biased regimens without that pair by -0.125, including a never-administered one. Modeling co-administered pairs' interactions removed the leakage. The share of a regimen's pairs never co-administered did not flag the failures (AUROC 0.37).
findings: Synergy on C+D (never co-administered): regimens containing C+D biased by 0.2, coverage 0.63 to 0.71; all others exact.
Synergy on A+B (co-administered): B+C and B+D biased by -0.125 (coverage 0.73 and 0.81) though neither contains A+B.
Interaction model for the co-administered pairs: unbiased when the synergy is on a co-administered pair, no help for C+D.
CMP-03.not_answered: One connected network, continuous outcome, fixed effect; no disconnection, covariate adjustment, selection procedures or formal synergy bound. Peer review has not been done.
CMP-03.design: Exact calculation on an eight-trial component network with three co-administered and three never co-administered component pairs; synergy of three magnitudes placed on one pair, both kinds, or all pairs; additive and prespecified-interaction models.
CMP-03.n_sim: Exact calculation: 4 synergy locations x 3 magnitudes x 2 models x 11 regimens
CMP-03.estimand: Effect of each two- to four-component regimen against placebo
methods_compared: component model with interactions for co-administered pairs

CMP-06.title: Miscoding the shared component of a bridged network costs identifiability, not accuracy; miscoding an internal component biases the bridged estimate
CMP-06.question: When the component coding of a disconnected network bridged by a shared component is wrong, does the error perturb the estimate or change what is estimable, and do sensitivity or probabilistic coding give honest intervals?
CMP-06.answer: Partly. When the bridge is real, coding the shared component as a distinct agent removed that trial's bridging information and, when it hit both bridging trials (up to 9.5% of replicates), made the target non-estimable, which a rank screen detects exactly; otherwise the estimate stayed unbiased with nominal coverage. The miscoding that left the row space intact, dropping an internal component, biased the target by about 0.8 SE and cut coverage to 0.83 given a miscoding. Probabilistic coding restored coverage (0.967 or more); coding sensitivity did too but was the whole line whenever a plausible coding broke the bridge.
findings: Connectivity-changing miscoding: coverage 0.943 to 0.945 given a miscoding and estimability; non-estimable 0.4% to 9.5%.
Connectivity-preserving miscoding: bias -0.095 to -0.105, coverage 0.826 to 0.868 given a miscoding (second null control failed).
A false bridge (a distinct agent coded as the shared component) is not identified under the true coding and was not simulated.
CMP-06.not_answered: One hand-built network, fixed-effect contrast-level fits, no covariate adjustment, synergy or Bayesian arm; independent miscoding within a small plausible set. Peer review has not been done.
CMP-06.design: Two subnetworks linked only by component A; subnetwork-2 codings miscoded independently with probability 0 to 0.3, either coding the shared component as a distinct agent (connectivity-changing) or dropping an internal component (connectivity-preserving); deterministic, sensitivity and probabilistic coding. 7 cells, 2000 replicates each.
CMP-06.estimand: Effect of component B across the gap
methods_compared: deterministic coding with a rank screen
coding sensitivity over the plausible set

CMP-11.title: Pooling standardized and unstandardized edges biases a component effect by exactly the untransported edges' share of the population difference
CMP-11.question: How large is the bias from pooling edges standardized to the target with edges left in their own populations, and is the two-stage route still the better practical choice than carrying every edge to the target?
CMP-11.answer: No. The two-stage bias equaled the aggregate edges' share of the pooled precision times the difference between their own-population and target effects (slope 0.97, R^2 0.997), zero only when modification or separation was zero. At 0.5 SD separation it reached -0.106 with coverage 0.27, and transporting every edge to the target had lower RMSE in all six such cells (0.038 to 0.089 against 0.047 to 0.113). Pooling conditional rather than marginal individual-data edges added up to 0.033 on the log odds ratio scale.
findings: b1 check: slope 0.967, intercept 0.0008, R^2 0.997 over 36 cells.
At 1 SD separation with a quarter of edges having individual data the two-stage bias exceeded the effect itself.
Transported arm coverage 0.90 to 0.96 (its variance ignores the shift's covariance with the individual-data edges); aggregate covariate laws were known exactly, so it is optimistic.
CMP-11.not_answered: Eight trials of one component rather than a component network; no one-stage component ML-NMR; aggregate covariate laws known; one network size. Peer review has not been done.
CMP-11.design: Eight trials of one component, a quarter to three quarters with individual data, aggregate trials separated from the target by 0 to 1 SD, effect modification absent or present, continuous or binary outcome; two-stage marginal and conditional pooling against a transported alternative. 36 cells, 1000 replicates each.
CMP-11.estimand: Marginal effect of one component in the target population
methods_compared: all edges transported to the target

CMP-12.title: Splitting a multi-arm trial's adjusted contrasts is conservative for one contrast and anticonservative for another
CMP-12.question: When a three-arm trial's population-adjusted contrasts share an arm and a weight vector, what is lost by treating them as independent, is the error ever anticonservative, and is dropping the trial cheaper?
CMP-12.answer: Ignoring the within-trial covariance errs in a direction set by the contrast, not by how the arms' effect modification aligns. The trial's own B-versus-C interval became conservative in every scenario, while the network A-versus-B interval, which borrows through the trial, fell below nominal in 15 of 30 scenarios. The shared-weighting part of the covariance took both signs but never reversed a contrast's error. Dropping the trial widened the network interval by 29% to 91%.
findings: Split, trial-alone d_BC: coverage 0.957 to 1.000, above nominal beyond 3 MCSE in 29 of 30 scenarios and below in none; DESIGN.md's alignment-sign prediction is withdrawn by its registered test.
Split, network d_AB: coverage 0.4 to 3.7 points below the stacked sandwich, below nominal beyond 3 MCSE in 15 of 30 scenarios against 0 for the stacked sandwich.
The shared-weighting covariance term was -22% to +15% of the Monte Carlo covariance, dominated by the shared-arm term.
Joint sandwiches recovered 0.76 to 1.15 (stacked) and 0.73 to 1.12 (weights fixed) of the Monte Carlo covariance; stacked trial-alone intervals covered 0.919 to 0.960.
Dropping the trial was unbiased and widened the network d_AB interval by a median 53%.
CMP-12.not_answered: Continuous outcome, linear modification, one three-arm trial in a fixed two-trial aggregate network; four-arm trials, the one-stage ML-NMR comparator and a bootstrap are not run, and target moments are fixed. Peer review has not been done.
CMP-12.design: Three-arm individual-data trial weighted by MAIC to a target, plus aggregate A-versus-C and B-versus-C trials in the target; 30 scenarios crossing effect-modification strength, its alignment across arms, target shift and shared-arm size; split, weights-fixed, stacked and drop analyses, network by generalized least squares.
CMP-12.estimand: d_AB, d_AC and d_BC in the target population

CMP-13.title: Separating within-trial from across-trial component effect modification
CMP-13.question: Component ML-NMR fits one shared interaction on a globally centered covariate, which algebraically forces the causal within-trial interaction to equal the confounded across-trial association. How much does that cost, when, and is the damage really caused by aggregate data as the catalog claims?
CMP-13.answer: Fitting one shared interaction matrix on a globally centered covariate is not pooling: for a binary modifier with study prevalence p_s it is algebraically identical to imposing that the causal within-trial coefficient equals the confounded across-trial one. In the model simulated, coverage of a nominal 95% interval for the causal interaction falls from 93.8% when that happens to be true to 17.2% when the two are equal and opposite, and further in networks whose contrasts move two components at once. Separating them costs about 5% in interval width and removes an order of magnitude of bias. The catalog's stated cause is incomplete: the loss is present with all twelve trials supplying individual data, so aggregate data are not necessary for it, but removing individual data roughly doubles the bias, so they amplify it.
findings: Coverage under the shared restriction degrades monotonically with the discordance between the within-trial and across-trial coefficients, from 93.8% at no discordance to 17.2% when they are equal and opposite, and it is worse in bundled component networks whose contrasts move two components at once than where every contrast isolates one.
Both separated estimators are nominal at every discordance examined, 92.6% to 96.3%, including under a nonlinear across-trial pattern where the linear split model is itself misspecified.

CMP-13 says aggregate studies cause the pull. With all twelve trials supplying individual patient data the shared model still has median absolute standardized bias 0.15 and coverage as low as 44.6%, so aggregate data are not necessary. But bias rises to 0.29 and coverage falls to 17.2% as individual data are removed, so they amplify it. The registered refutation threshold was narrowly missed (47% of cells against 50%) and we report that rather than moving it.

Where a component appears in no individual-data arm, the three methods behave in three different ways: the IPD-anchored estimator declines to report it in 100% of replicates; the shared model returns a confident -0.34 against a truth of zero, sourced entirely from the across-trial gradient; and the joint split returns intervals so wide that coverage approaches one, when it returns one at all.

A study-clustered sandwich, included so the comparison could not be won on the variance estimator, covered 75.4% to 92.4% where the shared model is correctly specified. With twelve clusters it is badly anticonservative, and it is reported as a finding rather than used as the comparator.
CMP-13.not_answered: The registered global analysis is uninformative and the regime split that produced a usable answer was prompted by observing that failure, so it is not prespecified. The general headline about component ML-NMR is not established: the likelihood and nuisance structures are not mapped onto the fixed- and random-effect specifications the implemented method offers, and free study-by-treatment effects or priors can absorb or alter the term the identity isolates. A maximum-likelihood analogue of component ML-NMR. Implemented ML-NMR is Bayesian and priors matter most where interactions are weakly identified, so the coverage numbers do not transfer to multinma; the algebra does, and therefore so does the direction. One binary modifier, a log link, a Poisson outcome, additive components with no synergy, no random treatment-effect heterogeneity, no inconsistency, and exactly reported study prevalences. Under the discordance patterns the split model is correctly specified, so the study measures the cost of an algebraically known restriction rather than establishing that real networks contain within/across disagreement or how large it typically is. Continuous or multiple correlated modifiers, misspecified aggregate covariate distributions, and time-to-event outcomes are untested. It does not touch IDN-05.
CMP-13.design: Twelve-trial two-component Poisson network with a binary effect modifier whose prevalence varies across studies, aggregate arms generated by exact integration. 320 scenarios crossing network structure, the discordance between within-trial and across-trial modification, IPD availability including a case where one component has no within-trial data at all, arm size and prevalence spread. 2000 replicates each.
CMP-13.estimand: Within-trial component interaction on the conditional log-rate scale

CMP-14.title: Prior-to-posterior contraction and effective likelihood rank measure information, not bias
CMP-14.question: CMP-14 asks for two default summaries, prior-to-posterior contraction per interaction and an effective likelihood rank, so an analyst sees when an aggregate-only interaction is held up by its prior. Would those summaries tell the analyst whether the reported interval covers?
CMP-14.answer: Not reliably, and the reason is structural. On an exact identity-link arm of 504 scenarios and a logit arm of 72, no threshold on contraction, on either effective-rank reading, or on the estimability screen separates scenarios whose 95% interval covers nominally from those that fail. The summaries are functions of Fisher information and the prior, so within one design they are exactly constant while coverage ranges from 0 to 0.96. They partly catch the failure they were designed for: contraction flags 59% of failures caused by a tight prior. They catch none of the 142 failures caused by a biased route, where the ecological route carries between-study confounding or the additivity route a synergy, because confounding moves the posterior mean and not its information. A clean contraction says the likelihood spoke, not that it was right. Every result is exploratory.
findings: All four registered statistics (contraction, target-level likelihood ratio, whole-model effective rank, estimability screen) take values shared by failing and nominal scenarios on both arms, so no threshold on any of them separates the classes. On E1 there are 251 failing and 169 nominal scenarios; on E2, 41 and 12.

On the identity link with known residual variance the posterior covariance does not involve the outcomes. Within one information state, spread, network size and prior, contraction, target ratio and effective rank are exactly constant across discordance and synergy levels while coverage ranges over 0.956.

Decomposed by cause (post hoc), 109 E1 failures come from a prior of SD 0.1 pulling a true interaction of 0.4 toward zero and 142 from a biased route. Contraction flags 58.7% of the first and 0% of the second; target ratio 41.3% and 0%; effective rank 56.0% and 0%.
Scenario pairs matched on spread, size and prior whose contraction differs by less than 0.02 differ in coverage by up to 0.951 on E1.

On the logit arm the rules score far better on average (contraction Youden 0.805 against 0.220 on E1) because 34 of its 41 failures sit at the tight prior and it has only 12 nominal scenarios. The overlap persists.

Three aggregate routes identify an interaction on the logit link, through differences in covariate means, covariate variances or baseline risk; only the first works on the identity link. None is randomized.
CMP-14.not_answered: Nothing here is confirmatory: E1 was computed before its protocol existed, E2's separation rules were rebuilt after its output was read, and the cause decomposition was added for the manuscript. E1 is exact for a design realized at its quadrature nodes and E2 is asymptotic, so no posterior was sampled and neither is an average over realized designs. The exact invariance of the summaries holds for known-variance Gaussian models; with estimated variances or random effects they would move with a departure and whether that movement could ever warn is untested. One target component, one covariate, one network geometry, a normal within-study covariate law on the logit arm, and departures acting on the mean only. The protocol went through thirteen rounds of critique; the manuscript has not been peer reviewed.
CMP-14.design: Exact computation on a four-component network, one scalar covariate, twelve arms in every state. The target interaction is identified by its own IPD trial, by a combination arm under additivity, by the between-study contrast in aggregate covariate means, by differing covariate variances (logit only), or not at all. E1: identity link, known variance, 504 scenarios crossing state, covariate spread, network size, interaction prior SD, discordance and synergy. E2: logit link, asymptotic, 72 scenarios.
CMP-14.n_sim: Exact and asymptotic computation: 504 E1 scenarios and 72 E2 scenarios, no Monte Carlo replicates
CMP-14.estimand: The within-trial interaction of the target component, true value 0.4; coverage of its nominal 95% interval
methods_compared: target-level likelihood to prior precision ratio

CMP-15.title: Calibrating the correlation does not fix the copula: the family moves a standardized contrast by up to 0.03 on the log odds and log hazard scales
CMP-15.question: Once a Gaussian copula's correlation is calibrated to the reported correlations, can the remaining error from copula family (asymmetry and tail dependence) move a target-standardized contrast?
CMP-15.answer: Yes, modestly on the log odds and log hazard scales and strongly on the log rate scale. With margins and correlation matched, the calibrated Gaussian erred by up to 0.034 on the log odds ratio and 0.032 on the log cumulative hazard ratio (above 0.02 in 5 of 16 primary cells), with opposite signs for lower- and upper-tail dependence, and by up to 0.63 on the log rate ratio. The error plateaued by 256 integration points. A wrong flexible family was worse than the Gaussian in 61% of comparisons, so the defensible report is an envelope over families.
findings: Identity link: every error exactly zero, as the second-order argument requires.
Uncalibrated versus calibrated Gaussian: at most 0.001 apart on the logit and complementary log-log scales.
Envelope over five families contained a t-copula truth outside them in 22 of 24 cells, median width 0.044.
Matched-correlation control narrowly failed: 0.0057 against a 0.005 tolerance, within the check's Monte Carlo error.
CMP-15.not_answered: Population-level; three exchangeable covariates with common margins; no mixed or discrete margins, vines or reconstruction uncertainty. Peer review has not been done.
CMP-15.design: Population-level numerical study: three covariates with normal or skewed margins, true Clayton, Gumbel or t copula at Pearson correlation 0.3 or 0.6, against calibrated and uncalibrated Gaussian and alternative-family reconstructions; identity, logit, log and complementary log-log links; integration order by randomized quasi-Monte Carlo.
CMP-15.n_sim: Population-level calculation: 10^6 draws per joint law, 2 margins x 2 correlations x 6 families
CMP-15.estimand: Target-standardized marginal contrast on the link scale
methods_compared: alternative copula families calibrated to the same correlation

CMP-16.title: Sharing one heterogeneity parameter across a bridged network cost little; the interval method mattered more
CMP-16.question: When two subnetworks of a bridged network have different between-study heterogeneity, does a shared tau give the bridged contrast valid intervals, and do stratified or shrunk alternatives do better at realistic study counts?
CMP-16.answer: Largely yes for a contrast that sums both subnetworks. With one subnetwork five times as heterogeneous, shared, stratified and shrunk heterogeneity models covered within 0.016 of each other (shared 0.906 to 0.932 and stratified 0.917 to 0.943 across 3 to 12 studies per subnetwork), because a shared tau overstates one part's variance and understates the other's. The undercoverage came from ignoring uncertainty in tau: Hartung-Knapp intervals covered 0.97 to 0.997 at three studies, at about 1.5 times the width.
findings: Registered rule: mixed; shared coverage never below 0.90 in the registered cells, lowest 0.897 elsewhere.
Every Wald interval covered about 0.90 to 0.92 at a 5:1 ratio with three studies per subnetwork.
The shared tau estimate sat between the two true values.
CMP-16.not_answered: A contrast drawing on one subnetwork only would carry the shared tau's error without the offset; frequentist REML without priors; no residual-variance arm or IPD. Peer review has not been done.
CMP-16.design: A bridged contrast summing two subnetworks' pooled effects; heterogeneity ratio 1, 2 or 5 in the bridging or the other subnetwork; 3, 6 or 12 studies each; shared, stratified and shrunk REML heterogeneity with Wald and Hartung-Knapp intervals. 15 cells, 2000 replicates each.
CMP-16.estimand: Bridged contrast formed as the sum of two subnetworks' pooled effects

CMP-18.title: Adding time-constant component hazard ratios mispredicted a combination's RMST when effects were delayed or follow-up differed
CMP-18.question: When two components have different time profiles of effect and their trials differ in follow-up, does adding their time-constant hazard ratios predict the combination's RMST, and does a piecewise extension fix it?
CMP-18.answer: No. With both component effects delayed, adding time-constant hazard ratios overstated the combination's 3-year RMST gain by 0.055 years (truth 0.405, coverage 0.88); a piecewise model reduced the bias to 0.017. With delayed and waning components and follow-up of 1.5 versus 3 years, the time-constant prediction was biased by -0.102 (coverage 0.82) and the piecewise model by -0.072 (coverage 0.91), because neither can learn a late effect the shorter trial never observed. With equal follow-up and effects summing to a constant, the time-constant model was accurate.
findings: Registered rule: neither model nominal where it mattered (piecewise 0.906 at unequal follow-up).
A constant hazard ratio moves benefit earlier than a delayed one, and RMST credits early benefit.
Constant effects: both models unbiased with coverage 0.93 to 0.94.
CMP-18.not_answered: Two single-component trials rather than a component network; no disconnection or population adjustment; one piecewise extension; one horizon. Peer review has not been done.
CMP-18.design: Trials of each component against control with constant, jointly delayed, or delayed-versus-waning effects and equal or unequal follow-up; stratified Cox with time-constant or piecewise component effects predicting the combination's 3-year RMST difference. 4 cells, 500 replicates each.
CMP-18.estimand: 3-year RMST difference of the component combination versus control

CMP-20.title: The aggregate Poisson likelihood is biased by the exposure-rate covariance, and exposure-weighted covariate moments remove the bias
CMP-20.question: The aggregate Poisson likelihood multiplies an arm's total exposure by its mean modeled rate, which is exact only when exposure and rate are uncorrelated. The error is the factor 1 + rho CV(T) CV(lambda) per arm. How much bias does that put on a transported rate ratio at plausible levels of differential follow-up, and do exposure-weighted covariate summaries remove it?
CMP-20.answer: No, the covariance cancels only when it is common to both arms. The bias followed the identity log{(1 + rho1 CV1(T) CV1(lambda)) / (1 + rho0 CV0(T) CV0(lambda))} (slope 0.994); at plausible dispersions with a differential correlation of at least 0.2, 27 of 64 cells had material bias or undercoverage, with bias up to 0.14 on the log rate ratio and coverage down to 0.17. Integrating aggregate arms over exposure-weighted covariate moments removed the bias everywhere (largest 0.008). Even with zero correlation the unweighted likelihood undercovered at large dispersions (0.84), because the finite-sample covariance is not zero.
findings: Identity check over 208 cells: slope 0.994 (SE 0.002), largest deviation 2.9 MCSE.
Exposure-weighted moments: bias at most 0.008, coverage 0.908 to 0.965; borrowed exposure slope: bias at most 0.015 but coverage down to 0.69 because the slope's uncertainty is ignored.

Null control failed on coverage (0.838 to 0.957 at zero correlation), not bias; positive control's cell selection corrected after the run; sensitivity range did not contain cells with positive treated-arm correlation (coverage down to 0.71).
CMP-20.not_answered: One covariate, one lognormal exposure law, no overdispersion, the same exposure mechanism in both studies; the likelihood is the study's own code, not multinma. Peer review has not been done.
CMP-20.design: A minimal anchored network, individual data on A versus C and arm totals on B versus C, with lognormal exposure solved so each arm's exposure-rate correlation and dispersions take registered values exactly. 234 attainable cells crossing the control-arm correlation, its difference in the treated arm, CV of exposure, CV of the rate and arm size; unweighted, exposure-weighted and borrowed-slope integration and a sensitivity bound. 1000 replicates per cell.
CMP-20.n_sim: 1000 per cell, 208 main cells and 26 control cells
CMP-20.estimand: Target-population log marginal rate ratio, B versus C
methods_compared: moments tilted by a borrowed exposure slope
sensitivity interval over a declared correlation range

CMP-21.title: An MNAR shift moved an anchored transported contrast in a direction that differed from dataset to dataset, but the tipping set was almost always one interval
CMP-21.question: When an MNAR shift in imputed effect-modifier values enters a transported anchored contrast through several routes, is the contrast monotone in the shift, and is the tipping point a single value?
CMP-21.answer: Partly. The tipping set was a single interval in at least 96% of replicates (non-single 3.0% to 4.4%, under the registered 5%), so a single tipping point sufficed here. But the routes offset only on average: the mean slope of the anchored contrast against the MNAR shift was -0.004 to 0.030, while per dataset its SD was 0.10 to 0.14 and it was positive in 48% to 62% of datasets. The direction in which an MNAR departure moves the contrast was not predictable from the design, so sensitivity analyses must explore both directions.
findings: Registered branch: cancellation without non-unique tipping sets (flat curves in up to 6.4% of replicates with differing missingness).
Curves were non-monotone over the shift range in 77% to 80% of replicates but crossed the decision threshold in more than one interval in at most 4.4%.
The decision reversed somewhere in [-1.5, 1.5] in 29% to 30% of replicates.
CMP-21.not_answered: Two anchored individual-data trials rather than a disconnected component network; one imputation per shift; congenial imputation; one MNAR mechanism; tipping set defined by the point estimate's sign. Peer review has not been done.
CMP-21.design: Two anchored individual-data trials with MNAR missing modifier values (equal or differing missingness), imputation plus a sensitivity shift over [-1.5, 1.5], STC standardized over a target law with a fixed or data-derived SD. 4 cells, 500 replicates each.
CMP-21.n_sim: 500 per cell, 4 cells, 31 shift values each
CMP-21.estimand: Marginal log odds ratio B versus A in the target, as a function of the MNAR shift
methods_compared: imputation plus shift with STC standardization, integration law fixed or from completed data

CMP-22.title: Which trials supply individual data, and what selection on it does
CMP-22.question: When the trials that supply individual data are selected on observed trial variables or on their own effect modification, how biased is the interaction evidence, does combining with aggregate trials help, and can a leave-IPD-out diagnostic reveal it?
CMP-22.answer: Selection of which trials supply individual data on an observed trial variable caused no bias, but selection on the trials' own effect modification biased the within-trial interaction evidence by up to 0.14 (true 0.3), with coverage down to 0.59. Combining with the across-trial association in all trials halved the bias. A leave-IPD-out influence diagnostic did not respond to the selection, so the problem is invisible without a stated selection model.
findings: Selection on the observed trial variable only: within-trial bias -0.003 to 0.003.
Selection on the latent interaction: within-trial bias 0.027 to 0.142; combined 0.014 to 0.065.
Leave-IPD-out influence 0.026 to 0.046, varying with the IPD share but not with selection strength (correlation with bias -0.85 at half the trials supplying data).
CMP-22.not_answered: Pairwise continuous-outcome meta-analysis rather than component ML-NMR; no selection-model sensitivity analysis; one network size. Peer review has not been done.
CMP-22.design: Twelve trials with trial-specific interactions and IPD availability depending on an observed trial variable and on the latent interaction; within-trial and combined estimators; leave-IPD-out influence. 18 cells, 1000 replicates each.
CMP-22.estimand: Mean treatment-by-covariate interaction and the effect at covariate 1
methods_compared: pooled within-trial interaction from IPD trials

CMP-24.title: A diagonal-weight influence ranked studies correctly only with two-arm studies and heterogeneity held fixed
CMP-24.question: Does the diagonal-weight influence that cpaic's edge_influence() reports rank studies the way refitted leave-one-study-out references do, once multi-arm covariance and re-estimated heterogeneity enter?
CMP-24.answer: No, the refuting sentence fails; the registered verdict is not fit for ranking. The diagonal influence equaled the correct hat row for two-arm networks (difference 8e-15) and ranked studies well there with tau fixed at 0 (mean Spearman with refitted variance importance 0.95 to 0.97; top study missed in 5% to 6%). With three-arm studies and tau fixed, Spearman stayed at 0.90 to 0.92 but the top study was missed in 28% to 46% of networks, almost always because a three-arm study was promoted. With tau re-estimated, mean Spearman was 0.51 to 0.70, including two-arm networks, and the top study was missed in 20% to 59%.
findings: Post hoc: when the top study disagreed at tau 0, the diagonal's choice was three-arm in 98% to 100% of networks against 18% to 25% for the reference's, and its reference importance was a median 15% to 21% below the maximum; the misses were not near-ties.
In 8-study two-arm networks with tau 0.3, 259 of 365 studies with zero diagonal influence moved the estimate when removed, through the re-estimated tau alone.
Spearman with the absolute change in the estimate was 0.50 to 0.59 in every cell, including the exact case: influence measures leverage, not realized change.
CMP-24.not_answered: Standard network meta-analysis rather than component networks with population adjustment; study-level deletion; cpaic's formula reimplemented, not called; no fixed-tau reference; a block-weighted hat matrix was not tested; 120 of 6000 networks with singular refits dropped. Peer review has not been done.
CMP-24.design: Random four-treatment networks of 8 or 16 studies, two-arm only or with three-arm studies, tau 0 to 0.3; diagonal influence against leave-one-study-out variance importance and estimate change with tau re-estimated. 12 cells, 500 networks each.
CMP-24.estimand: Rank agreement between each study's diagonal-weight influence on the D versus A contrast and its refitted leave-one-study-out variance importance
methods_compared: leave-one-study-out refit of the correct model, tau re-estimated

CMU-02.title: Do prior-sensitivity diagnostics catch the analyses that are actually wrong?
CMU-02.question: In a population-adjusted network a proper prior yields a proper posterior even where the likelihood identifies nothing, so a narrow interval can reflect the prior rather than the evidence. The diagnostics that would expose this exist. What are their operating characteristics: do they flag the analyses whose intervals actually miss the truth, and how often do they cry wolf?
CMU-02.answer: At the thresholds the literature suggests, they miss most of it. Pairing each warning with whether that replicate's own interval missed, a composite of four diagnostics has sensitivity 0.37 at a false-alarm rate of 0.16, falling to 0.13 outside two engineered geometries; the one sensitive rule fires on half the sound analyses too. Used as continuous scores the same statistics reach AUC 0.51 to 0.78, so this is a failure of thresholds rather than of the statistics. What no threshold repairs is that these diagnostics measure the prior's influence while the harm comes from the prior's location: with disconnected evidence and a tight prior four standard deviations from the truth, going from 100 to 400 per arm drops the warning rate from 0.98 to 0.01 while coverage stays near zero.
findings: Prespecified verdict: diagnostics fail at the thresholds the literature suggests. Composite sensitivity 0.366 (MCSE 0.002), false alarm 0.158; 0.127 and 0.025 outside the engineered positive controls.

Sensitivity and specificity trade off completely. Tight-and-loose prior refitting catches 0.83 of misses outside the controls and fires on 53% of covered replicates. Contraction, the prior-only benchmark and power-scaling keep false alarms low and catch almost nothing.

The composite adds almost nothing over its best component: 0.366 against contraction's 0.363, at a higher false-alarm rate. Requiring two of four rules to agree neither buys specificity nor recovers sensitivity.

More data makes the warning quieter while the answer stays wrong. Disconnected evidence, tight prior, true interaction four prior SDs away: coverage near zero at both sample sizes, warning rate 0.98 at 100 per arm and 0.01 at 400. Contraction is what every diagnostic reads as reassurance.

A first implementation measured power-scaling by posterior mean shift and found sensitivity 0.000 everywhere. That was our error: with a zero-centred prior, scaling the prior up and the likelihood down give identical posterior means, so the standard rule can never fire. Measured distributionally it works, and the verdict does not depend on the amendment.
The structural rank screen is the only rule with no false alarms at all, and it is blind to every failure where the contrast is estimable and the answer is still wrong.
CMU-02.not_answered: The other half of CMU-02, wiring these diagnostics into released software, is untouched; neither multinma nor cpaic is run. The model is conjugate Gaussian with an identity link, a correctly specified linear mean and known variances, so nothing transfers directly to a non-conjugate posterior where MCMC error enters and the diagnostics behave differently. Only automated thresholds are evaluated; a plot read by an experienced analyst is a different instrument. Thresholds were taken from the source literature and not tuned. CMP-14 is touched only for the generic aggregate-only interaction, not for component models, and IDN-06 is not addressed at all because this design contains no within-versus-between discrepancy.
CMU-02.design: A conjugate Gaussian population-adjusted network in which every piece of evidence reduces without loss to a normal observation, so the posterior and every power-scaled posterior are exact and no diagnostic is contaminated by MCMC noise. 120 scenarios crossing the evidence available about the weakly identified treatment, arm size, whether the truth agrees with the zero-centered prior, prior scale, and the target population. 2000 replicates each.
CMU-02.n_sim: 2000 per scenario, 240,000 datasets and 480,000 contrast evaluations
CMU-02.estimand: Target-population marginal C versus B mean difference, and the conditional interaction coefficient

COV-02.title: The adjustment set is a property of the scale
COV-02.question: Does the set of covariates whose imbalance changes a transported contrast differ between the risk difference, risk ratio, marginal odds ratio and conditional odds ratio scales?
COV-02.answer: The covariates a transported contrast depends on change with the scale, but not in the nested way DESIGN.md predicted. Prognostic non-modifiers never affected the conditional log odds ratio and affected some marginal scale by more than 5% in 13 of 24 scenarios, the risk difference included, because with a logistic model every prognostic variable modifies the risk difference; the risk difference was in fact the most sensitive scale (median 4.5% change per unbalanced prognostic variable, against 1.6% for the marginal odds ratio). Sets differed between the risk difference, marginal and conditional odds ratio in 10 of 24 scenarios, below the registered threshold of half, so the refuting sentence holds as registered.
findings: Registered verdict: refuting sentence HOLDS (sets differ in 42% of scenarios against a 50% threshold).
Marginal odds ratio set containing the risk-difference set (DESIGN.md's prediction): 19 of 24 scenarios.

Median relative change from one unbalanced prognostic variable: 0.045 (risk difference), 0.035 (log risk ratio), 0.016 (marginal log odds ratio), 0 (conditional log odds ratio). Near-null contrasts inflate relative changes.
COV-02.not_answered: No time-to-event scale; no sampling or estimation of the sets; independent normal covariates. Peer review has not been done.
COV-02.design: Population-level numerical study: logistic outcome with 0 to 3 conditional modifiers and 2 or 6 prognostic non-modifiers, two prognostic strengths and two imbalances; each covariate's omission scored by its relative change in the target contrast on four scales.
COV-02.n_sim: Population-level calculation, 24 scenarios, 10^6 common random draws each
COV-02.estimand: Target A-versus-C contrast on the risk difference, log risk ratio, marginal and conditional log odds ratio scales
methods_compared: mean balancing with each covariate in turn left unbalanced

COV-03.title: What an anchored comparison must balance on a non-collapsible scale
COV-03.question: On the log odds ratio scale a purely prognostic covariate changes the marginal effect. Does an anchored MAIC that balances only covariate means, as practice does, leave material bias, and does balancing the variance of the prognostic index remove it at acceptable cost in effective sample size?
COV-03.answer: Yes. On the log odds ratio scale a difference in the spread of prognosis between trials biases an anchored MAIC that balances only means by up to 0.11, even with no effect modification. Balancing variances or the variance of the prognostic index removes the bias, but when the source is less dispersed than the target the loss of effective sample size makes RMSE worse than not balancing. G-computation was unbiased with the lowest RMSE throughout.
findings: MAIC on means biased by 0.05 to 0.11 in the 12 primary anchored scenarios, beyond 0.05 (95% Monte Carlo interval) in 9; registered verdict CONFIRMED.
Unadjusted anchored bias on the exact population bias: slope 0.981 (SE 0.018).
Balancing variances cut the bias to at most 0.08 (0.02 in all but one scenario) but dropped effective sample size to 44 to 284 of 1000 when the source index variance was half the target's.
G-computation: largest absolute bias 0.024 anchored and 0.020 unanchored, lowest RMSE in every primary scenario.
COV-03.not_answered: Independent normal covariates and a correctly specified outcome model favor G-computation. Hazard ratios, skewed covariates and augmented estimators not run; MAIC intervals treat weights as fixed. Peer review has not been done.
COV-03.design: Anchored and unanchored binary-outcome comparisons, 108 cells crossing prognostic strength, the source-to-target ratio of prognostic index variance, target mean shift and effect modification; five methods including MAIC on means, on means and variances, on the prognostic index variance, and G-computation. 1000 replicates per cell.
COV-03.estimand: Marginal log odds ratio, B versus A, in the target population
methods_compared: MAIC on means and the prognostic index variance

COV-04.title: Shrinkage priors on interactions do not give honest intervals for a transported effect
COV-04.question: Do posterior intervals from shrinkage or selection priors on treatment-by-covariate interactions keep frequentist coverage for the transported effect when the whole procedure is repeated?
COV-04.answer: No. Continuous shrinkage does not select, but its intervals still undercovered: 95% posterior intervals for the transported effect covered 0.794 to 0.948 with an empirical-Bayes ridge prior and 0.868 to 0.959 with a hierarchical normal prior, against 0.939 to 0.955 for a flat prior. When the interactions the target weights push the effect the same way, their joint shrinkage biases the transported effect (up to 0.19) and the narrower interval does not carry the bias. Integrating the prior scale recovers only part of the loss.
findings: Worst cell, three moderate modifiers at 100 per arm: empirical-Bayes ridge 0.794, hierarchical normal 0.868, spike-and-slab averaging 0.908, median-probability model 0.785, flat 0.954.
Plugging in the fitted prior scale costs up to 0.074 coverage relative to integrating it; the remainder is prior-truth conflict at a fixed nonzero truth.
The median-probability model's conditional interval, the Bayesian form of DEC-11's selection, was the worst prior at 300 per arm (0.840 with three moderate modifiers).
With one strong modifier at 300 per arm every prior except the median-probability model covered at least 0.948.
COV-04.not_answered: Continuous outcome with conjugate priors; no horseshoe, heredity constraints or projection-predictive selection; aligned modifiers only, no null scenario. Peer review has not been done.
COV-04.design: Continuous-outcome STC with eight candidate interactions, one strong or three moderate modifiers, two sample sizes; flat, empirical-Bayes ridge, hierarchical normal, spike-and-slab averaging and median-probability-model priors. 4 cells, 1000 replicates each.
COV-04.estimand: Target-population mean difference, A versus C, -0.5 + 0.5 times the sum of the interactions

COV-01.title: Coverage of an STC interval after selecting effect modifiers on the same data
COV-01.question: When effect modifiers are selected on the analyzed data before an STC, does an interval that treats the selected model as fixed keep its coverage, and does resampling the whole procedure restore it?
COV-01.answer: Selecting effect modifiers on the analyzed data (interactions with p < 0.2) left the naive STC interval covering 0.887 to 0.927, because its SE ignored which model was selected; a bootstrap that repeats the selection restored 0.938 to 0.968. Lasso at the one-standard-error penalty dropped real modifiers and coverage fell to 0.33 with three modifiers at 1000 per arm. Fitting all candidate interactions kept coverage at 0.93 to 0.96.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: naive coverage after significance selection below 0.93 beyond Monte Carlo error in some scenarios (0.887 to 0.927); bias at most 0.046.
Whole-procedure bootstrap: 0.938 to 0.968.
Lasso (lambda 1se) kept on average 0.01 to 0.15 interactions; coverage as low as 0.333 and bias about -0.2 with three real modifiers.
The shortfall was not monotone in sample size with three modifiers (largest at 300 per arm), as registered.
COV-01.not_answered: STC only; MAIC-based selection, overlap, larger candidate sets and target-summary uncertainty not run; 400 replicates. Peer review has not been done.
COV-01.design: G-computation STC with six candidate modifiers, five selection rules (all, oracle, none, p < 0.2, lasso), naive and whole-procedure bootstrap intervals, three sample sizes and one or three true modifiers. 400 replicates per cell.
COV-01.n_sim: 400 per scenario, 2,400 in total, each with a 60-resample bootstrap
COV-01.estimand: Target-population marginal log odds ratio, A versus C

COV-09.title: The same covariate name, two instruments
COV-09.question: When the source and target measure a matched effect modifier with different instruments, how is the MAIC estimate biased, does a reliability correction recover it, and can a bounded analysis over declared instrument differences contain the truth?
COV-09.answer: MAIC's bias from a modifier measured by different instruments follows a closed form in the instruments' offsets, slopes and the source reliability. A reliability correction removes it only when both trials use the same instrument; with differing instruments it left bias up to 0.18 and could undo a chance cancellation. An envelope of corrected intervals over declared instrument differences covered the truth at 1.4 to 2.9 times the naive width.
findings: Naive bias on its closed form: slope 0.992 (SE 0.009) over 45 scenarios; zero without modification.
Shared instrument: reliability-corrected bias within 3 MCSE in 12 of 12 scenarios with modification.

Differing instruments: corrected bias above 0.05 in 15 of 18 scenarios, up to 0.176; at reliability 0.6 a target offset cancelled the attenuation in the naive analysis (bias -0.018) and the correction removed the cancellation (0.172).
Bounded analysis over declared instrument differences: coverage 0.967 to 1.000, width 1.36 to 2.93 times naive.
COV-09.not_answered: Linear instruments and identity link only; misclassification of binary covariates and bridging-sample correction not run; target sampling error absent. Peer review has not been done.
COV-09.design: Continuous-outcome MAIC with a latent modifier recorded by the source and reported by the target through linear instruments with offsets, slopes and error; 45 cells crossing instrument pairs, source reliability and modification strength; naive, reliability-corrected and bounded analyses. 1000 replicates per cell.
COV-09.estimand: Target-population mean difference, A versus C
methods_compared: bounded analysis over declared instrument differences

COV-10.title: Interaction coefficients have their own consistency equation
COV-10.question: When direct and indirect paths carry opposing treatment-by-covariate interactions, does the pooled network meta-regression mask the modifier while the effect-consistency check passes, and can an interaction-consistency check detect it?
COV-10.answer: Opposing interactions on direct and indirect paths attenuate the pooled network meta-regression interaction toward zero, fully at the balance point and partly across a continuum, while the effect-consistency check stays at its null rate. The target effect was biased by 0.13 to 0.30 whether or not the covariate was selected. A direct interaction-consistency check detects it when studies per path and covariate spread are adequate (up to 1.00) and has little power otherwise (0.16 with two studies and narrow spread).
findings: Effect-consistency check flag rate 0.094 to 0.107 in every interaction-inconsistent scenario without effect inconsistency (blindness confirmed).
Refuting sentence fails: partly opposing interactions biased the target by -0.13 to -0.26.

Cancelling configuration: pooled interaction mean near 0 but replicate SD 0.13 to 0.67 against model SE 0.03 to 0.38 (1.5 to 4.2 times), so the Wald test selected the covariate in 31% to 88% of analyses.
Interaction-consistency check power 0.16 to 1.00, rising with studies per comparison and covariate spread.
COV-10.not_answered: Stylized triangles with continuous estimates; design-by-treatment interaction model and larger networks not run. Peer review has not been done.
COV-10.design: Triangle networks with path-specific interaction slopes (consistent, partly opposing, cancelling), two to eight studies per comparison, two covariate spreads and effect inconsistency absent or present; consistency meta-regression, modifier selection, interaction and effect consistency checks. 36 cells, 2000 replicates each.
COV-10.estimand: C versus A effect at a covariate value of 1.5, with the AC path's modification as truth
methods_compared: consistency network meta-regression with covariate selection

COV-12.title: Reconstructing a target covariate from a median: when the mean is enough and when it is not
COV-12.question: When a target publication reports a skewed covariate as a median with IQR or range, how much error does reconstructing its marginal put into a target-standardized contrast, and is that error a function of the reconstructed mean alone?
COV-12.answer: Under an identity link with linear effect modification, yes: the contrast error is exactly the modification coefficient times the mean error. Under a logit link, no: the mean explains only 60% of the error's variance, because the reconstruction's spread and shape also enter. With strong skew and a reported range, a normal reconstruction biased the contrast by more than 1 on the identity scale and 0.4 on the log odds ratio scale, growing with sample size; a lognormal matched to the reported quantiles kept bias below 0.1.
findings: Registered test, contrast error net of the sample floor regressed on the modification coefficient times mean error: identity link slope 1.000, R^2 1.000; logit link slope 0.246, R^2 0.597.
Normal reconstruction (Wan et al.) with strong skew and a range: bias 1.15 (identity) and 0.42 (logit) at 200 patients; 2.15 (identity) at 1000, since the range grows with n.
Quantile-matched shifted lognormal: largest bias 0.092 across all 72 scenarios.
Without skew the lognormal matcher is not free: sampling asymmetry in the reported quantiles triggers it, and its bias reached 0.08, against 0.005 for the normal reconstruction.
COV-12.not_answered: One covariate with a known conditional model; estimated outcome models and multivariate marginals with dependence (CMP-15) are not covered. The lognormal matcher suits right skew only. ML-NMR integration is represented by direct integration. Two cells were run before a regressor correction and discarded unread. Peer review has not been done.
COV-12.design: A known conditional model integrated over target marginals reconstructed from a sample median with IQR or range; 72 scenarios crossing link, skewness, reported summary, target size (50 to 1000) and modification strength.
COV-12.estimand: Target-population marginal treatment effect (difference or log odds ratio)
methods_compared: integration over the target's own sample (floor)

COV-14.title: Covariate sets that differ across comparators, and the ranking read from them
COV-14.question: When one individual-data trial is compared with several aggregate comparators that report different covariates, does adjusting each contrast for everything it reports give a worse ranking than adjusting all contrasts for the common set, even though each contrast is less biased?
COV-14.answer: Neither adjustment rule protects the ranking. The common (intersection) set ranked better in 15 of 36 scenarios and the maximal sets in 19; which wins depends on whether the omission bias pushes a lower-ranked comparator past a higher one, which the data do not show. The registered inversion was not confirmed in the primary scenarios, whose pattern turned out to widen the top comparator's lead, but held in all six Fawsitt-like scenarios with similar populations. The intersection's per-contrast bias was a median 2.4 times the maximal. A bounded analysis over the other comparators' reported means covered at least 0.93 with similar comparator populations at little extra width.
findings: Registered primary (strongest covariate missing for the top comparator, similar populations, tied effects): maximal sets lower on both bias and wrong-top-rank probability in 3 of 3 scenarios; verdict MAXIMAL VINDICATED.
Fawsitt-like pattern, similar populations: intersection lower wrong-top-rank probability in 6 of 6 scenarios, up to 0.94 against 0.31.
The difference between the two analyses did not predict a wrong top rank (AUROC 0.567).
Bounded interval coverage at least 0.929 with similar comparator populations at 1.00 to 1.99 times the maximal width; 0.678 at worst with dispersed populations. Maximal-set coverage fell to 0.086.
COV-14.not_answered: Continuous outcome and independent covariates; non-collapsible outcomes, correlated omissions, a single ML-NMR network fit and overlap as a factor were not run. Three reporting patterns sample but do not exhaust where omissions can fall. Peer review has not been done.
COV-14.design: Unanchored MAIC of one trial against four comparators with nine covariates, 36 cells crossing reporting pattern, prognostic strength, similarity of comparator populations and separation of true effects, plus 8 control cells; maximal, intersection and bounded analyses. 1000 replicates per cell.
COV-14.estimand: B_k versus A mean difference in each comparator's population, and the ranking of the four
methods_compared: bounded interval over other comparators' reported means

DEC-01.title: Do estimation and decision rankings of population-adjustment methods agree?
DEC-01.question: When population-adjustment methods are ranked by the decisions their estimates lead to rather than by RMSE, does the ranking change, and how does it depend on where the truth sits relative to the decision threshold?
DEC-01.answer: For a threshold on a known side of the truth, yes: near the threshold in poor-overlap scenarios the RMSE and expected-loss rankings correlated at only 0.45, and the disagreement was reproducible, not noise. It came from the direction of bias: a biased method decided wrongly far less often when its bias pointed away from the threshold (0.11 against 0.64). Averaged over the two sides of the threshold, as an analyst who does not know the truth must, the rankings agreed (0.93, the same best method in every poor-overlap scenario). RMSE is therefore an adequate proxy for decision error unless the side of the threshold is known.
findings: Registered primary (near threshold, poor overlap, symmetric loss): mean Spearman correlation 0.45 (95% bootstrap interval 0.29 to 0.60); RMSE-best also loss-best in 38% of strata; verdict CONFIRMED.
Exploratory: split-half reliability of the rankings 1.00 (RMSE) and 0.96 (expected loss) in poor-overlap scenarios, against a cross-measure correlation of 0.44.
Biased methods (|bias| > 0.05), threshold 0.1 from the truth: wrong-decision probability 0.114 with bias pointing away from the threshold and 0.635 toward it.
Exploratory: loss averaged over both sides of the threshold correlated with RMSE at 0.93 (distance 0.1) and 0.96 (0.3) in poor-overlap scenarios.
DEC-01.not_answered: Decision on the relative effect only, without a net-benefit model; one source of replicates (COV-03) and five methods; no ML-NMR; priors on the side of the threshold not modeled. Peer review has not been done.
DEC-01.design: Re-scoring of COV-03's 108,000 stored replicates (five methods) against thresholds 0.1 or 0.3 above or below the truth, with loss ratios 1, 2 and 5; rank correlation between RMSE and expected-loss rankings by stratum, plus exploratory split-half reliability and two-sided averaging.
DEC-01.n_sim: 108,000 replicates re-scored (108 scenarios x 1000), 5 methods, 12 threshold-loss settings
DEC-01.estimand: Wrong-decision probability and expected loss of adopting B over A, against the true recommendation
methods_compared: MAIC on the prognostic index variance

DEC-02.title: Which analysis choice flips a decision
DEC-02.question: Within one decision question, which analysis choices most often flip a population-adjusted recommendation, and how does that compare with the change in the question when the target population changes?
DEC-02.answer: The choices are ordered rather than dominated by one. Near a decision threshold, adjusting or not flipped a population-adjusted decision in 36% of analyses, weighting against an outcome model in 20%, linear against quadratic STC in 13% and MAIC on means against means and SDs in 7%. Changing the target population moved the true log odds ratio by 0.39 to 0.59, more than any estimator choice moved the estimate, so the target belongs to the question, not the sensitivity analysis.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: the top flip rate (0.363) was less than three times the next (0.202).
Far from the threshold (0.3) flip rates fell by more than half for every choice.
True log odds ratio across target covariate means 0.3 to 1.2: changes of 0.39 to 0.59 across modification patterns.
DEC-02.not_answered: No prior or bridge factor; decision on the relative effect only; one outcome type. Peer review has not been done.
DEC-02.design: Re-scoring of DIA-08's stored replicates: decision flips between the two options of four analysis choices at thresholds near and far from the truth, and the true effect across three target populations.
DEC-02.n_sim: 32,000 stored replicates from DIA-08 re-scored at four thresholds
DEC-02.estimand: Decision to adopt B (estimated log odds ratio below a threshold) against the true decision

DEC-11.title: Coverage of an STC interval after selecting effect modifiers on the same data
DEC-11.question: When effect modifiers are selected on the analyzed data before an STC, does an interval that treats the selected model as fixed keep its coverage, and does resampling the whole procedure restore it?
DEC-11.answer: Selecting effect modifiers on the analyzed data (interactions with p < 0.2) left the naive STC interval covering 0.887 to 0.927, because its SE ignored which model was selected; a bootstrap that repeats the selection restored 0.938 to 0.968. Lasso at the one-standard-error penalty dropped real modifiers and coverage fell to 0.33 with three modifiers at 1000 per arm. Fitting all candidate interactions kept coverage at 0.93 to 0.96.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: naive coverage after significance selection below 0.93 beyond Monte Carlo error in some scenarios (0.887 to 0.927); bias at most 0.046.
Whole-procedure bootstrap: 0.938 to 0.968.
Lasso (lambda 1se) kept on average 0.01 to 0.15 interactions; coverage as low as 0.333 and bias about -0.2 with three real modifiers.
The shortfall was not monotone in sample size with three modifiers (largest at 300 per arm), as registered.
DEC-11.not_answered: STC only; MAIC-based selection, overlap, larger candidate sets and target-summary uncertainty not run; 400 replicates. Peer review has not been done.
DEC-11.design: G-computation STC with six candidate modifiers, five selection rules (all, oracle, none, p < 0.2, lasso), naive and whole-procedure bootstrap intervals, three sample sizes and one or three true modifiers. 400 replicates per cell.
DEC-11.n_sim: 400 per scenario, 2,400 in total, each with a 60-resample bootstrap
DEC-11.estimand: Target-population marginal log odds ratio, A versus C

DEC-17.title: Which evidence drives a network contrast changes across the plausible range of heterogeneity
DEC-17.question: Are the contribution shares that attribute a network meta-analysis contrast to its studies and comparisons stable over the plausible range of the between-study variance, or does conditioning on its point estimate change which evidence appears to drive the result?
DEC-17.answer: No. In a four-study loop network with 5:1 within-study variances, the leading contributing comparison changed across the profile-likelihood interval for tau in 38% to 42% of networks, and the largest single study share moved by about 0.15 on average; with equal within-study variances shares did not move at all. REML put tau at zero in 30% to 67% of four-study networks. The instability comes from the data's inability to distinguish values of tau, not from bias in its estimate.
findings: Leading study changed across the tau interval in 38% to 42% (loop, 4 studies), 27% to 31% (8), 6% to 13% (16).
Shares at tau-hat differed from shares at the true tau by 0.01 to 0.05 on average.
In the star network comparison-level shares are fixed at 50% by construction; study-level leadership changed in 15% to 18% of eight- and sixteen-study networks.
DEC-17.not_answered: One contribution measure (absolute hat-matrix row), three treatments, two-arm studies, frequentist only. Peer review has not been done.
DEC-17.design: Three-treatment star and loop networks of 4, 8 or 16 two-arm studies with equal or 5:1 within-study variances and true tau 0, 0.1 or 0.25; hat-matrix contribution shares at tau-hat, over its profile-likelihood interval and at the true tau. 36 cells, 1000 networks each.
DEC-17.estimand: Contribution shares of studies and comparisons to the C versus B contrast
methods_compared: range of shares over the tau profile interval

DEC-28.title: The covariate value at which the better treatment changes is often not estimable as a point, and borrowed precision can make its interval wrong
DEC-28.question: Is the covariate boundary between two treatments' optimality well enough determined at achievable interaction precision to report as a point, and do standard intervals for it hold when interaction information comes partly from between-trial variation?
DEC-28.answer: No. From one trial of 400 patients at a moderate interaction the exact (Fieller) 95% confidence set for the boundary was unbounded in 66% to 69% of replicates, while the delta-method interval was always finite and covered as little as 0.86 at the weakest interaction. Borrowing interaction precision from aggregate trials at different covariate means (81% of the precision) made the sets bounded, but a between-trial ecological term of 0.1 cut their coverage to 0.68 to 0.70 for a boundary away from the trials' mean covariate value. Treating by the point estimate at the moderate interaction lost 31% to 95% of the value of individualized treatment with one trial.
findings: Fieller sets bounded from one trial: 84% to 85% at interaction 0.3, 31% to 34% at 0.15, 7% to 9% at 0.05.
The pointwise probability that A is better, thresholded at 0.5, is the plug-in rule; its (0.025, 0.975) region is the Fieller set, so it changes the report, not the decision.
With the ecological term, combined-estimator coverage 0.68 to 0.70 at boundary 1.5 and 0.92 to 0.93 at 0.5; individual-trial coverage 0.95.
At interaction 0.05, treating by the estimated boundary did worse than treating everyone with the better treatment on average (regret share up to 3.6).
DEC-28.not_answered: Two treatments and one modifier; no modifier selection; closed-form frequentist estimators rather than ML-NMR; declared linear ecological term. Peer review has not been done.
DEC-28.design: One individual-data trial plus five aggregate trials; interaction 0.3, 0.15 or 0.05, two boundary positions, an ecological term absent or present; within-trial and combined estimators; delta-method and Fieller intervals, regret and the pointwise optimality map. 12 cells, 2000 replicates each.
DEC-28.n_sim: 2000 per cell, 12 cells, two estimators each
DEC-28.estimand: The boundary x* = -delta/beta between two treatments' optimality, and regret of treating by its estimate

DIA-02.title: The reported weight panel cannot see where support is missing
DIA-02.question: Every member of the overlap panel MAIC reports (Kish ESS, ESS percentage, entropy efficiency, maximum weight, top-share) is a symmetric function of the weights, so none can depend on where in covariate space the source fails to cover the target. Does that blindness matter in an ordinary covariate law, or do weight concentration and support geometry move together tightly enough that the panel is an adequate proxy?
DIA-02.answer: It matters. Two source populations that remove the same mass at the same threshold, one in the effect-modifying coordinate and one in a prognostic coordinate, give panels that agree to within 1.6% while one estimate is biased by 0.016 on the marginal risk difference and the other by less than 0.0001, and material error is 24 times as frequent in the first. Across the two placements every panel member sits within 0.005 of chance; region-specific ESS separates them almost perfectly and sliced optimal transport cost at 0.73, but a convex hull distance maximized over coordinates is as blind as the panel. The registered within-arm primary outcome reads the other way (panel 0.574, best geometric 0.592, rule returns refuted) because within one arm the hole placement is fixed and the outcome measures sampling noise, not geometry. Both readings are reported. Balance on the omitted moment, the comparator most likely to overturn the headline, was never fairly tested.
findings: The manipulation works in a plain multivariate normal law. With strong effect modification, a hole in the modifying coordinate biases MAIC's marginal risk difference by 0.0164 and a same-sized hole in a prognostic coordinate by -0.0001, while every panel member agrees between the two arms to within 1.6%. The refuting sentence, that such a counterexample needs configurations that do not occur, fails.

Across the two hole placements, over 16,000 replicates, the best panel member separates them at 0.505 against 0.5 for chance, standard error 0.004. Region-specific ESS separates them at 1.000 and sliced optimal transport cost at 0.726. Convex hull distance, though it reads position, separates at 0.503 because it is a maximum over coordinates and both arms remove an identical wedge.

The registered primary, AUROC against material error within the high-modification arm, returns refuted: best panel member 0.574, best geometric 0.592, a gap of 0.018 against a registered materiality of 0.10. Within one arm every replicate shares the hole placement, so the registered outcome asks which replicate drew a bad sample, and a concentration measure answers that as well as anything. The registered outcome was the wrong measurement for the proposition; it is reported as registered, not relabeled.

Two of three controls failed on parts of the grid. At eight covariates and moderate overlap MAIC's own error exceeds the 0.03 material threshold in 0.289 of replicates with no hole at all, the same threshold-below-noise defect IDN-05 documented. Leaving the modifier's second moment unmatched breaks the symmetry the manipulation rests on and the panels diverge by up to 91%. The analysis runs on the 12 of 48 cells the controls leave, all at good overlap.

Two of the three ESS definitions implemented are the same statistic when weights are normalized, so the measured comparability spread is Kish against entropy ESS: median 1.55 times, 90th percentile 3.50, maximum 15.5 on identical data.
A post hoc probe prices the rescue of the failed strata by the upper Clopper-Pearson bound: 48,000 source records at dim3/moderate and 192,000 at dim8/moderate. It was not run.
DIA-02.not_answered: Balance on the omitted moment, the free check registered as most likely to overturn the headline, was not tested: every cell where it had anything to see was removed by the matched-multiset control. Region-specific ESS was handed the easiest instance, since the region it examines is the region the hole empties, so its near-perfect separation is an upper bound; a hole in a high-modification region the analyst did not think to examine is untested and there it would fail like the panel. No diagnostic is calibrated to a threshold. The analysis subgrid was chosen by a mechanical rule written after the run was read. The realized high-modification hole holds 22% of the modification mass against a registered 25%. MAIC weights only, a binary outcome, normal covariates, one rectangular hole, good overlap only after the null control, and two of the three published ESS definitions. Peer review has not been done.
DIA-02.design: Target covariates independent standard normal in 3 or 8 dimensions; source shifted by 0.25 or 0.60 with a wedge above the 90th percentile removed from the effect-modifying coordinate, from a prognostic coordinate, or not at all. Binary outcome on the logit scale with one modifying coordinate. 48 cells crossing dimension, hole placement, overlap, balancing set and modification strength, source size 16,000. Nine diagnostics scored by AUROC within the high-modification arm and across the two hole placements.
DIA-02.n_sim: 2000 per cell, 96,000 replicates; 24,000 on the 12 cells the controls leave
DIA-02.estimand: Target-population marginal risk difference, and material error above 0.03 as the classifier label

DIA-03.title: Effective sample size tracks the error an analysis got by chance better than the error it got from adjusting on the wrong covariates
DIA-03.question: Every population adjustment arrives with a panel of numbers beside it: effective sample size, the same figure as a percentage, the largest weight, standardized differences before and after adjustment, a distance between populations. A committee reads them as evidence about whether to believe the estimate, and a widely quoted rule says to worry below an effective sample size of about 30 to 35. Scored as classifiers of realized error, with discrimination and calibration, against known truth and under a declared distribution of analyses, what are they worth?
