DIA-03.answer: At the level at which a diagnostic is actually read, one analysis at a time, effective sample size tracks the error a study got by chance far better than the error it got from adjusting on the wrong covariates: AUROC 0.847 against the outcome-noise component and 0.813 against chance covariate imbalance between the source arms, both of which are functions of the covariates, the assignment and the weights, against 0.653 for the transport component that adjustment exists to remove. At the quoted cutoff of 35 it catches between a quarter and a third of material errors in every misspecification stratum, 0.309 where an effect modifier is omitted and the omission is diagnosable in principle, at specificity 0.926. No evaluated fixed cutoff met the registered requirement of sensitivity 0.80 at specificity 0.50 in every stratum. Three of the panel's members are provably one statistic, since ESS/n = 1/(1+CV^2(w)) exactly and area under the ROC curve is invariant to monotone transformation; a fourth, the post-weighting balance on matched moments, is zero at the solution of the calibration equations and among converged analyses cannot discriminate anything. On a decision-curve basis every rule in the panel is beaten by scrutinizing every analysis, up to an action threshold of 0.3.
findings: Prespecified verdict: the panel does not classify realized error at the thresholds in use. No rule reached sensitivity 0.80 with specificity 0.50 in every misspecification stratum. ESS below 35 reaches sensitivity 0.251 to 0.326 across strata at specificity 0.909 to 0.926.

The mechanism, registered before the run and holding at the level of a single analysis: effective sample size discriminates the outcome-noise component at AUROC 0.847 and the transport component at 0.653, a gap of 0.194, and the arm-imbalance component at 0.813. The two it reads well are the two that are functions of the covariates, the assignment and the weights, which is what the panel is built from.

Peer review changed this claim and the paper's title. Scored against SYSTEMATIC transport bias with the design cell as the unit, rather than against the realized transport component of one replicate, effective sample size reaches 0.808 rather than 0.653. That analysis does not rescue the panel either: the statistic that is identically zero reaches 0.708 on it, because 128 cells is a small sample in which the bias and every diagnostic move along the same overlap axis. Both levels are reported and the title now claims only the replicate-level result.

The panel is smaller than it looks, by algebra rather than by simulation. ESS, ESS as a percentage and the coefficient of variation of the weights had identical areas under the ROC curve to 0.0e+00 within a fixed source size. The matched-moment balance statistic never exceeded 1.4e-14 and its apparent AUROC of 0.550 is discrimination of floating-point residual, not of balance.

Silence is where the damage is. Across the 88 cells the ESS rule never fires in, the material-error rate runs from 0.045 to 0.835. The registered version of this claim, a spread across the cells it does fire in, was not met (0.150 against a prespecified 0.30) because those cells are all bad. A first draft called the silent-cell span a stronger version of the registered claim; peer review established that both spans are variation in predictive value, which moves with prevalence and case mix, so neither is a test of whether a threshold transports. That promotion is withdrawn and the leave-one-factor-level-out calibration is the evidence on transportability.

Decision-curve analysis: at action thresholds up to 0.3, flagging every analysis beats every rule in the panel. From 0.4 upwards three distinct statistics beat both alternatives, relative effective sample size, pre-weighting imbalance and Mahalanobis distance; the absolute cutoff that gets quoted is not among them at any threshold examined.

The same statistics work when they measure the actual gap. Pre-weighting imbalance predicts the unadjusted comparison's transport error at AUROC 0.891, against 0.655 for the same statistic applied to MAIC. These diagnostics are informative about the problem and uninformative about the solution: weighting sets to zero the very quantity they measure.

Our proposal, converting residual imbalance on a measured but unadjusted covariate into the units of the estimand with the source-estimated interaction, reaches 0.937 against the transport component over the diagnosable set where effective sample size as a percentage reaches 0.851. That gain of 0.086 misses the 0.10 we registered and is reported as a miss. Inside the omitted-modifier stratum alone the plain balance check on unmatched covariates beats it, 0.946 against 0.938, because there the covariate is always a modifier and converting imbalance into effect units only adds estimation noise. The conversion earns its keep exactly when the analyst does not know whether the unmatched covariate matters.

An adversarial critique of the design before the run found two arithmetic errors in the protocol: the dispersion factor was not the pure variance instrument it was described as wherever the cross-moment channel was on, and the target trial's variance was understated by a factor of two to three. Both were confirmed numerically and corrected before any result was seen.

Round one of review found the load-bearing claim of the paper wrong, and all three reviewers found it independently. The arm-imbalance component uses no outcome at all, and the noise component's variance is exactly sigma^2 (1/ESS_A + 1/ESS_C), so a weight statistic is its natural summary rather than merely correlated with it. Round one also found that the calibration split was perfectly confounded with the dispersion factor, because cells are enumerated with that factor varying fastest; leave-one-factor-level-out replaced it and the previous claim that overlap statistics calibrate worse than weight statistics was withdrawn as an artifact.
DIA-03.not_answered: The second half of DIA-03 is untouched: no PSIS-LOO is computed at any hierarchical level and grouped study-level leave-one-out is no more implemented here than in the packages, so the mismatch between the level at which cross-validation is reported and the level at which the prediction is made remains open. DIA-06 is answered only in part; two estimator families and no adjustment are compared on identical replicates, but ML-NMR, NMI, doubly robust estimators and flexible learners are absent. The outcome is continuous with an identity link, which is what buys the exact error decomposition and is also the largest restriction: nothing here transfers to non-collapsible effect measures or time-to-event outcomes, where part of the error is a collapsibility artifact rather than an adjustment failure. Covariates are normal, comparisons are anchored, conditional constancy holds, and target moments are exact. The deployment weights are a declared judgment and nothing in this program measured them, which is why the primary results are within strata.
DIA-03.design: An anchored indirect comparison with a continuous outcome and an identity link, chosen so that the realized error of a linear estimator splits exactly into arm imbalance, transport error and outcome noise, so each diagnostic can be scored against each component separately: two of the three are functions of the covariates, the assignment and the weights, which is what the panel is built from, and the third is what adjustment exists to remove. 128 cells crossing an omitted effect modifier, a cross-moment modifier that no baseline table could reveal, overlap, source size, how correlated the omitted modifier is with the adjustment set, and a target dispersion ratio that destroys effective sample size while adding no bias where the modifier structure is correct. 4000 replicates per cell, four estimators. Primary results are reported within misspecification strata rather than over a mixture, so no investigator-chosen frequency enters the headline.
DIA-03.estimand: Transported A versus C mean difference in the target superpopulation; the anchored A versus B contrast as a secondary reference
methods_compared: MAIC matching means and standard deviations

DIA-07.title: Where the individual data sit decides the error of a population-adjusted network contrast at the same total sample size
DIA-07.question: At a fixed total sample size, does the error of a population-adjusted network contrast depend on the network's topology and on which trial supplies individual data, beyond total information?
DIA-07.answer: No. At 1200 patients in every network, the probability of getting the sign of the decision contrast wrong ranged from 0.36 to 0.93 across four topologies and positions of the one individual-data trial (moderate modification, target shifted one SD), and the spread exceeded 0.10 in every scenario. An individual-data trial off every path to the contrast carried zero weight and changed nothing; standardizing one edge could raise the bias (0.20 to 0.30 in a line network) by removing an error that had offset the others.
findings: Star network: IPD on A-B or A-C has zero weight on D versus A; only the direct A-D trial removes the bias.
Line network: standardizing B-C gave an unbiased estimate by cancellation of the remaining edges' modification differences.
Coverage ranged from 0.02 to 0.95 across configurations at the strongest modification.
DIA-07.not_answered: Deterministic calculation; continuous outcome, linear modification, four hand-built topologies, one IPD trial, fixed-effect model; no generated topology families, component networks or ML-NMR. Peer review has not been done.
DIA-07.design: Exact calculation: four-treatment line, star, loop-with-tail and two-path networks with 1200 patients in total, one individual-data trial standardized to the target on each edge in turn, effect modification of three strengths and two target shifts.
DIA-07.n_sim: Exact calculation: 4 topologies x all placements x 3 modification strengths x 2 target shifts
DIA-07.estimand: D versus A mean difference in the target population
methods_compared: network meta-analysis with one trial standardized to the target, placed on each edge in turn, across four topologies

DIA-08.title: Does the generator's effect-modification structure decide the method ranking?
DIA-08.question: When effect modification departs from the shared linear form most simulations use, does the ranking of population-adjustment methods change?
DIA-08.answer: Not at these magnitudes. The RMSE ordering under shared linear modification was reproduced under threshold, interaction and quadratic modification at every overlap level (rank correlation 0.9 to 1.0, the only change a swap between the two worst methods). STC with linear interactions ranked first everywhere even though the departures biased it by up to 0.12, because weighting methods lost more to variance at poor overlap. The generator decides a ranking only when a departure's bias exceeds the precision differences between methods.
findings: Registered verdict REFUTED: Spearman correlation between the linear and departure orderings 0.9 to 1.0 in all 9 comparisons (the analysis first classified one exact 0.9 as below threshold through floating point; rounding fixed it).
STC linear bias under the interaction and quadratic departures at target mean 1.2: 0.12 and 0.10, coverage 0.94; RMSE 0.34 against 0.53 to 0.56 for MAIC.
Quadratic STC did not overtake linear STC under the departures it models: its extra variance exceeded the bias it removed.
Skewed covariates with linear modification reordered methods as much as any modification departure.
DIA-08.not_answered: Moderate departure magnitudes only; treatment-specific, subnetwork and within-versus-between departures need a network and were not run; no ML-NMR. Peer review has not been done.
DIA-08.design: Anchored binary-outcome comparison with reported moments held fixed; linear, threshold, interaction and quadratic modification at three overlap levels, plus skewed covariates; unadjusted, two MAIC and two STC specifications ranked by RMSE and compared by rank correlation. 2000 replicates per cell.
DIA-08.estimand: Marginal log odds ratio, B versus A, in the target population
methods_compared: STC with quadratic and product interactions

DIA-09.title: Competing risks: a correct hazard ratio, a wrong cumulative incidence
DIA-09.question: When population adjustment transports a time-to-event outcome with a competing cause, does a correctly transported cause-specific hazard ratio give the right cumulative incidence in the target, and what repairs it?
DIA-09.answer: For competing risks, population adjustment transports the cause-specific hazard ratio (unbiased in every scenario) but not the cumulative incidence a decision model uses: when the target's competing hazard differed from the source's beyond the measured covariate, A's absolute incidence at 2 years was biased by up to 0.20 (true value 0.25) with coverage near zero. The between-arm difference was affected less. Recalibrating the competing hazard to the target's reported competing-event proportion removed the bias. The registered rule (bias beyond 0.05 wherever the competing hazard differed) was met in 20 of 24 method-scenarios; the exceptions were at half the competing hazard, with bias 0.041 to 0.049.
findings: Cause-1 log hazard ratio: bias within 3 MCSE in 16 of 16 scenarios, at most 0.013.

A's cumulative incidence from MAIC or STC: bias 0.13 to 0.20 with coverage at most 0.03 at four times the competing hazard; -0.04 to -0.06 at half; registered verdict NOT CONFIRMED (20 of 24 method-scenarios beyond 0.05).
A-minus-C difference: bias at most 0.049.
Recalibrated competing hazard: bias at most 0.004; coverage 0.851 to 0.943 for the absolute incidence and 0.943 to 0.972 for the difference.
DIA-09.not_answered: Only the competing-risks family; cure fractions, recurrent events, ordinal and joint net-benefit outcomes not run. Exponential hazards, one covariate, no ML-NMR. Peer review has not been done.
DIA-09.design: Anchored transport with exponential cause-specific hazards, the target's competing hazard differing from the source's beyond the measured covariate; 16 cells crossing that difference, effect modification and overlap; MAIC, cause-specific STC and STC with the competing hazard recalibrated to the target's reported competing-event proportion. 1000 replicates per cell.
DIA-09.estimand: Target cumulative incidence of the event of interest at 2 years under A, and its A-minus-C difference; cause-1 log hazard ratio
methods_compared: cause-specific STC with the competing hazard recalibrated to target data

DIA-10.title: Reconstruction error from a digitized Kaplan-Meier curve was too small to change which method ranks best for RMST
DIA-10.question: When the comparator arm must be reconstructed from a published Kaplan-Meier figure, does the reconstruction error change which method performs best, as it would if it penalized likelihood-based methods more, or does it only shift every method's error?
DIA-10.answer: Yes, for RMST within follow-up the omission is harmless. Reconstructing the comparator arm from a pixel-rounded Kaplan-Meier figure changed neither the ranking of Kaplan-Meier and Weibull RMST (same in all 8 cells) nor any method's RMSE by more than 1%: it added 0.003 to 0.040 months of bias to Kaplan-Meier RMST and 0.006 to 0.059 to Weibull RMST against a sampling SD of about 0.5 months. The likelihood-based method was more exposed, as predicted, but immaterially.
findings: Share of mean squared error attributable to reconstruction: -0.6% to 0.1% (KM), -0.4% to 0.9% (Weibull), zero within Monte Carlo error.
Reconstruction bias was upward and largest at coarse resolution, from reading drops at pixel-column centers.
Integrating the digitized curve directly performed as well as reconstruction.
DIA-10.not_answered: Reconstruction error only; RMST within follow-up only (extrapolated survival and hazard ratios not ranked); no human digitization variability; other access mechanisms not simulated. Peer review has not been done.
DIA-10.design: OUT-13's publication and reconstruction model; Kaplan-Meier and Weibull RMST on true and reconstructed data and the digitized curve integrated directly; fine or coarse figures, 6-monthly risk table or none, spread or clustered censoring. 8 cells, 1000 replicates each.

DIA-13.title: Do bias mechanisms in an unanchored MAIC combine additively?
DIA-13.question: When an omitted confounder, comparator outcome misclassification and covariate measurement error act together on an unanchored MAIC, is their joint bias the sum of their separate biases, and does a one-at-a-time analysis bound it?
DIA-13.answer: No. An omitted confounder and misclassification of the comparator's outcome interacted by up to 0.16 on the log odds ratio scale: with both at their largest the joint bias was about half the sum of the separate biases, and with the confounder reversed the joint bias had the opposite sign to that sum. Measurement error in a matched covariate combined nearly additively with either. The joint bias exceeded the largest single-mechanism bias in 22 of 36 combinations, so one-at-a-time analyses neither add up to nor bound it.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: median interaction 30% of the summed separate biases where two or three mechanisms acted.
Confounder by misclassification: interaction up to 0.163; other pairs at most 0.005.
Joint bias beyond the largest single-mechanism bias in 22 of 36 combinations; mechanisms partly cancelled in 16.
DIA-13.not_answered: Population-level only; no bias-analysis procedure, false reassurance or tipping sets; three mechanisms; selection and correlated parameters not varied. Peer review has not been done.
DIA-13.design: Population-level numerical study: exact bias of the MAIC limit over 45 combinations of three mechanisms, with interaction terms by inclusion-exclusion.
DIA-13.estimand: Marginal log odds ratio, B versus A, in the target (unanchored)
methods_compared: unanchored MAIC limit under combinations of three bias mechanisms

QBA-22.question: When an omitted confounder, comparator outcome misclassification and covariate measurement error act together on an unanchored MAIC, is their joint bias the sum of their separate biases, and does a one-at-a-time analysis bound it?

DIA-14.title: A quantitative bias analysis verdict scored as a classifier
DIA-14.question: How often does a QBA declare a MAIC decision robust when the true bias would reverse it, how does that depend on the elicited region rather than the method, and does oracle recovery reveal it?
DIA-14.answer: A QBA's robust verdict is only as good as the elicited region. When the region contains the true bias the grid never reassures falsely (an exact property); with elicitation errors scaled to the region it reassured falsely at most 17% of the time the true bias reversed the decision, but with the common region centered at zero bias it did so 78%, 37% and 9% of the time at half-widths 0.05, 0.15 and 0.3. Probabilistic QBA avoided false reassurance by calling 62% to 85% of sound decisions fragile. Oracle recovery was nominal throughout and revealed none of this.
findings: Exact checks: zero grid false reassurance in every replicate whose region contained the true bias and at exclusion probability 0.

Primary (exclusion 0.1, half-width 0.15): grid false reassurance 0.008 (symmetric) and 0.020 (understated); false fragility 0.333 and 0.279. Probabilistic QBA 0.000 and 0.710 to 0.748. Neither dominated.
Refuting sentence fails: oracle coverage 0.951 to 0.961 in every scenario while grid false reassurance under a zero-centered region was 0.776, 0.370 and 0.092.
The probabilistic QBA's own Monte Carlo error (1000 draws) changed its verdict in 0.9% to 1.6% of analyses.
DIA-14.not_answered: One scalar bias parameter; effect modification and overlap not varied; the elicitation model is assumed. Peer review has not been done.
DIA-14.design: Unanchored MAIC with an unmeasured binary confounder; elicited bias regions with exclusion probability set directly, three error directions and three widths; grid and probabilistic QBA scored on false reassurance and false fragility; 18 cells, 2000 replicates each.
DIA-14.n_sim: 2000 per scenario, 36,000 in total, each scored under 21 elicitation settings
DIA-14.estimand: Robustness classification: whether the decision at the true bias equals the unadjusted decision
methods_compared: deterministic grid (equivalent to bounds and tipping point for one scalar bias)

DIS-03.title: A baseline-risk bridge across a disconnected network
DIS-03.question: When disconnected subnetworks are linked through exchangeable baseline risks, does study-level design nuisance pass into the cross-gap contrast, and can design covariates separate it from prognosis?
DIS-03.answer: A baseline-risk bridge transports whatever makes the subnetworks' baselines differ. When a design nuisance (such as an endpoint definition) coincided with the subnetwork it passed one for one into the cross-gap contrast (bias 0.2 to 0.7) and no adjustment was possible. When a quarter of trials used the other definition, adjusting for it removed the nuisance but not prognostic drift between subnetworks (bias 0.19 to 0.20).
findings: Refuting sentence fails: without crossover, adjustment possible in 0% of analyses and bridge bias 0.207 to 0.712.
With 25% crossover and no drift, adjusted bias within 0.003.
With prognostic drift 0.2, adjusted bias 0.191 to 0.204.
DIS-03.not_answered: Study-level summaries, no Bayesian arm-based model or commensurate prior, one design covariate. Peer review has not been done.
DIS-03.design: Two subnetworks with prognostic drift, a design nuisance on the baseline and a design covariate overlapping the gap or not; exchangeable-baseline bridge with and without design adjustment. 24 cells, 2000 replicates each.
DIS-03.estimand: Cross-gap contrast C versus A on the log odds scale
methods_compared: bridge adjusted for a design covariate

DIS-11.title: A predictive winner among models that share a false bridge
DIS-11.question: When candidate models share a bridge assumption across a disconnected network, does a predictive criterion computed on observed trials rank them by their cross-gap error?
DIS-11.answer: No. Candidate models that share the bridge had identical cross-gap bias (0 to 0.5 across scenarios), and the leave-one-trial-out winner was set by within-subnetwork structure: meta-regression won when a trial covariate changed the contrast, the common-effect model when not, with the same distribution at every bridge error. A predictive criterion on observed trials cannot rank models by an error they share.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: winner distribution independent of the bridge error (chi-square p 0.68 and 0.44).
Cross-gap bias -0.007 to 0.499, identical across candidates.
DIS-11.not_answered: Frequentist predictive densities rather than LOO-PSIS on ML-NMR; no grouped leave-subnetwork-out or synthetic deletion; population comparison not simulated. Peer review has not been done.
DIS-11.design: Two disconnected subnetworks linked by exchangeable baselines with a design nuisance of varying size; three candidate models sharing the bridge ranked by leave-one-trial-out predictive density. 6 cells, 1000 replicates each.
methods_compared: leave-one-trial-out log predictive density over three candidate models sharing an exchangeable-baseline bridge

DIS-21.title: A matched bridge's admission threshold sets its bias: at the threshold used in practice the bridged contrast was biased by twice the true effect
DIS-21.question: How do the bias of a matched bridge across a disconnected network and the existence of the bridged comparison depend on the admission threshold, expressed in multiples of the distance between arms of one randomized trial?
DIS-21.answer: No. With trial populations shifted across the gap, the bridged contrast (truth -0.2) was biased by -0.03 at the within-trial arm distance, where the bridge existed in only 8% of replicates, -0.13 at three times it and -0.44 at ten times it, near the threshold used in practice, where it always existed and its interval never covered. An index omitting the most prognostic covariate was biased by -0.25 even at the tightest threshold. Pooling pairs that reuse arms made intervals undercover even without bias (0.76 at ten units with good overlap).
findings: Bias moved by 0.19 to 0.39 across thresholds at which the bridge existed at least a fifth of the time (poor overlap).
Probability the bridge exists at the within-trial distance: 46% (good overlap) and 8% (poor), all covariates in the index.
Study-level baseline heterogeneity (SD 0.1) lowered coverage at every threshold, since no covariate distance sees it.
DIS-21.not_answered: Monte Carlo networks only, no real-network deletions; one distance with two covariate sets; no component network meta-analysis bridge; admitted pairs pooled as independent. Peer review has not been done.
DIS-21.design: Two disconnected subnetworks of six trials; cross-gap control arms matched on covariate means at thresholds of 1 to 20 within-trial units; good or poor overlap, an index with or without the most prognostic covariate, study-level heterogeneity absent or present. 8 cells, 2000 replicates each.
DIS-21.n_sim: 2000 per cell, 8 cells, 8 thresholds on the same data
DIS-21.estimand: Cross-gap mean difference A versus B through a matched C-D bridge
methods_compared: matched bridge at thresholds of 1 to 20 within-trial distance units, two covariate indices

EST-06.title: When two sponsors' MAICs disagree: how often, why, and which common target resolves it
EST-06.question: When two sponsors run MAIC on the same two trials, each weighting its own data to the other trial, how often do their conclusions reverse, how much of that is a real difference in target population rather than sampling error or differing adjustment sets, and which common-target remedy recovers the decision population's effect?
EST-06.answer: Reversal is mostly a real target difference and it is common: with the modifier's zero-effect point between the two populations, sponsors disagreed in sign in 23% to 56% of analyses at separations up to 1 SD and modification up to 0.4, and moving the point outside the populations cut that by a median 0.31. The two sponsors' estimates are correlated, which a reversal calculation must use. Under linear modification the plain average of the two analyses is as accurate for the midpoint population as transporting both trials there.
findings: Between-minus-outside reversal probability exceeded 0.20 in 11 of 18 common-set configurations (median 0.31); the refuting sentence, that reversals need extreme configurations, fails.
Correlation between the two sponsors' estimates 0.14 to 0.99; a bivariate normal with that correlation predicted the reversal probability within 0.036, and ignoring it erred by up to 0.44.
A sponsor that left the modifier out of its weights was biased by 0.10 to 0.91 against its own target.
Transport of both trials to a declared population and the average of the two analyses: largest bias 0.024 and 0.027, median RMSE 0.231 and 0.239.
EST-06.not_answered: Linear modification and a continuous outcome; with nonlinear modification or a non-collapsible scale the average is not the midpoint effect. The arbitrated indirect comparison and measurement differences between trials were not run. Peer review has not been done.
EST-06.design: Two trials with linear modification of one treatment, analyzed by two sponsors each weighting its own trial to the other's population; 108 scenarios crossing separation, modification strength, the position of the zero-effect point, trial sizes and adjustment sets, plus controls; transport of both trials to a declared population and the average of the two analyses as remedies.
EST-06.estimand: B-versus-A mean difference in each sponsor's target population and in a declared decision population
methods_compared: transport of both trials to a declared population

EST-11.title: Scored against its own target, the unadjusted comparison ranked best; against a declared target it ranked worst
EST-11.question: Does scoring each method against its own implicit target give the same method ranking as scoring against a declared decision target, across a menu of targets and with correct or misspecified second-stage transport?
EST-11.answer: No. The method with the lowest RMSE against its own implicit target differed from the one with the lowest RMSE against the declared decision target in 5 of 6 cells. The unadjusted Bucher comparison, scored against the mixture of populations it estimates, won the native metric everywhere because it has the least variance, and was biased by 0.13 to 0.25 against the declared target in five cells. When the comparator's modification differed from the individual-data treatment's, methods native to the comparator trial's population missed a declared target one covariate SD away by 0.11, and a two-stage transport assuming shared modification did not remove it.
findings: Target mismatch (exact): 0 to 0.003 with shared modification; up to 0.11 for MAIC and STC and 0.25 for Bucher without it.
Among adjusted methods RMSE differences were within 0.03 against a sampling SD of about 0.25, so their order is not resolved at 300 per arm.
Two-stage STC removed the mismatch under shared modification and matched MAIC's bias when it failed.
EST-11.not_answered: Three declared targets, one covariate, one sample size, exact target moments, four methods; no ML-NMR or ML-UMR. Peer review has not been done.
EST-11.design: Anchored binary-outcome comparison with individual data on A versus C and published B versus C; three declared targets, B sharing A's modification or not; Bucher, MAIC, STC and two-stage STC; mismatch term exact, estimation term from 1000 replicates per cell, 6 cells.
EST-11.n_sim: 1000 per cell, 6 cells; mismatch term by quadrature
EST-11.estimand: Marginal log odds ratio B versus A in a declared target population
methods_compared: two-stage STC to the declared target

EST-12.title: Treatment hierarchies across target populations
EST-12.question: Does a treatment hierarchy move more across plausible target populations than across sampling variability, so that a hierarchy must name its population?
EST-12.answer: Yes: where effect modification changed the true ranking across plausible targets, the estimated hierarchy moved 1.6 to 2.4 places per treatment across targets against 0.1 to 1.4 places across sampling replicates, so a hierarchy must name its population. But estimated hierarchies also moved 0.2 to 2.1 places across targets where the true ranking did not change, through the uncertainty of meta-regression slopes away from the data's center, so a changed hierarchy is not by itself evidence of population dependence.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: in all 10 scenarios with a true rank change, movement across targets exceeded movement across replicates beyond Monte Carlo error.
Spurious movement across targets with no true change: 0.23 to 2.07 places per treatment.
Best treatment misidentified at an outer target in up to 70% of analyses (two trials per comparison, closely spaced effects).
EST-12.not_answered: Study-level meta-regression rather than ML-NMR; P-scores only; one covariate; fixed-effect. Peer review has not been done.
EST-12.design: Star networks of five treatments against a reference with treatment-specific linear modification; fixed-effect meta-regression and P-scores at three targets; rank movement across targets against movement across independent replicates. 24 cells, 1000 replicates each.
EST-12.estimand: Treatment ranks (P-scores) at declared target covariate means
methods_compared: fixed-effect meta-regression with P-scores at each target

HET-02.title: Matched single-arm studies built against one comparator arm
HET-02.question: When several single-arm studies are each matched to the same comparator arm and their pseudo-contrasts enter a network as independent, how much does that overstate precision, and does it change the conclusion?
HET-02.answer: Entering pseudo-contrasts built against one comparator arm as independent counts that arm once per study. Its reported SE shrank as studies were added while the estimate's spread did not, so coverage fell from 0.88 with one study to 0.57 with eight (comparator arm of 50). Modeling the shared covariance kept coverage at 0.95. In this fixed-effect network the point estimate barely changed; the error is in the stated precision.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: naive coverage 0.567 to 0.884 with two or more pseudo-contrasts; correct 0.945 to 0.955.
Naive SE with a comparator arm of 50: 0.137 (one study) to 0.059 (eight), against a true spread of 0.167 to 0.147.
Mean absolute difference between naive and correct point estimates small; sign disagreement rare.
HET-02.not_answered: Fixed-effect continuous network without a weighting step; heterogeneity and conflicting evidence, where the point estimate can also move, not run. Peer review has not been done.
HET-02.design: Network with two randomized trials and one to eight single-arm studies sharing one comparator arm; fixed-effect generalized least squares with the correct block covariance or with independence. 8 cells, 4000 replicates each.
HET-02.estimand: A versus C mean difference in the network
methods_compared: generalized least squares with the shared-arm covariance

HET-03.title: Shared and class-specific heterogeneity cannot be told apart below about 40 studies per class
HET-03.question: How many studies per class are needed before model comparison reliably distinguishes a shared between-study variance from class-specific ones?
HET-03.answer: No. Even with a fivefold difference in between-study variance, AIC chose class-specific variances in only 18% of networks with five studies per class, 40% with twelve and 79% with forty. Balanced selection accuracy reached 0.8 only at 40 studies per class and only for AIC; BIC and a likelihood-ratio test did not within 40. At the network sizes population-adjusted analyses use, the heterogeneity structure cannot be chosen from the data, so the shared default is untested rather than supported.
findings: Twofold variance ratio: separate structure chosen in at most 27% of networks by any criterion up to 40 studies per class.
AIC false-positive rate rose from 0.6% (2 studies per class) to 15% (40).
BIC with two studies per class chose separate variances under the null in 12% because its penalty log(2m-2) is below 2.
HET-03.not_answered: Two classes, contrast-level data, frequentist criteria; no Bayesian model comparison, informative priors, ML-NMR or class-specific treatment SD. Peer review has not been done.
HET-03.design: Two classes of 2 to 40 studies each with between-study variance ratio 1, 2 or 5; shared and separate REML fits compared by AIC, BIC and a likelihood-ratio test. 21 cells, 2000 replicates each.
HET-03.estimand: Probability of selecting the true heterogeneity structure

HET-04.title: A population difference arriving as inconsistency
HET-04.question: When the studies supplying the direct and indirect paths of a loop differ in an effect modifier, how often does unadjusted node splitting flag the population difference as inconsistency or miss a real conflict that the difference cancels, and what does an adjusted split achieve?
HET-04.answer: Unadjusted node splitting tests inconsistency plus population mismatch. With no true inconsistency it flagged 14% to 98% of analyses when the direct and indirect study sets differed in an effect modifier, and it fell to its null rate when the mismatch cancelled a real conflict. A split adjusted for the modifier held size (4% to 6%) and recovered some masked conflicts, but its precision fell as the gap between the study sets grew.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: unadjusted flag rate 0.141 to 0.982 with no inconsistency and differing populations; adjusted 0.041 to 0.058.
Exact masking: unadjusted 0.058 to 0.105; adjusted 0.074 to 0.254.
Adjusted inconsistency SE rose from 0.10 to 0.30 as the covariate gap went from 0 to 1 (four studies per comparison, modification 0.4); power against 0.2 fell from 0.54 to 0.12.
Unadjusted split at 0.10 even with no gap under modification 0.4, from covariate-driven heterogeneity.
HET-04.not_answered: Continuous study estimates, one loop, no Bayesian node split or marginalization to a named target. Peer review has not been done.
HET-04.design: Triangle networks with a covariate gap between the direct and indirect study sets, modification strength, true loop inconsistency and two or four studies per comparison; unadjusted and meta-regression-adjusted node splits. 54 cells, 2000 replicates each.
HET-04.estimand: Loop inconsistency factor for the B versus C contrast

HET-10.title: Interval coverage for population-adjusted synthesis with few studies
HET-10.question: How does interval coverage of population-adjusted random-effects synthesis depend on the number of studies, when one individual-data trial supplies the adjusted contrast for several aggregate trials?
HET-10.answer: Coverage fails in two ways. Meta-analyzing per-trial adjusted contrasts that reuse one individual-data trial as if independent lost coverage as trials were added (down to 0.55 at twelve trials with DerSimonian-Laird), because the shared error does not average out. Pooling the aggregate trials first and subtracting the transported contrast once fixed that; with DerSimonian-Laird it stayed within 0.93 to 0.97 from four trials, and Hartung-Knapp was conservative (up to 1.00) at two or three.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: coverage at two to four trials was 0.774 to 0.888 for the per-trial analysis and 0.909 to 0.962 for the two-step DerSimonian-Laird analysis.
Minimum trial count with coverage 0.93 to 0.97 at every heterogeneity level: 4 for two-step DerSimonian-Laird; none for the per-trial analyses or two-step Hartung-Knapp.
Per-trial analysis coverage fell with the number of trials even without heterogeneity.
HET-10.not_answered: Pairwise synthesis with one individual-data trial; continuous outcome; no one-stage or Bayesian analysis; one overlap level. Peer review has not been done.
HET-10.design: One individual-data trial transported by MAIC and 2 to 12 aggregate trials with heterogeneity; naive and two-step random-effects analyses with DerSimonian-Laird or Hartung-Knapp intervals. 18 cells, 2000 replicates each.
HET-10.estimand: B versus A mean difference in the target population

IDN-01.title: What each transitivity screen can see
IDN-01.question: Do the available transitivity screens (covariate dissimilarity, loop inconsistency, heterogeneity), run together, detect the violations that bias a network estimate, and can their pattern of flags identify the mechanism?
IDN-01.answer: No. Each screen sees one direction of violation, and an unmeasured modifier that makes one treatment look better in every comparison that includes it is invisible to all three: at size 0.4 it biased the network estimate by 0.40 with coverage near zero while the screens together fired at their null rate (0.28). Loop breaks and drift were detected with power rising in the number of studies, but the pattern of flags identified the mechanism poorly, and a measured modifier was always flagged although adjustment removed its bias.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: loop-consistent unmeasured modification of 0.4, any-screen detection 0.281 and 0.279 against 0.274 and 0.283 with no violation; bias -0.40.
Loop break of 0.4: detected in 0.77 (2 studies per comparison) and 0.98 (5); drift of 0.4: 0.95 and 1.00.
Measured modifier: dissimilarity flagged 100% of analyses; meta-regression bias at most 0.003.
Mechanism read from the flag pattern: loop breaks 43% correct, drift 34%; drift often triggered the loop test.
IDN-01.not_answered: Stylized triangle networks with continuous estimates; calendar drift as random shifts; abandonment records not scored. Peer review has not been done.
IDN-01.design: Triangle networks with two or five studies per comparison and five violation mechanisms, including a loop-consistent unmeasured modifier constructed to be invisible to every screen; 26 cells, 2000 replicates each; detection, bias, coverage and mechanism identification.
IDN-01.estimand: B versus C effect in a declared target population

IDN-05.title: A violation twice the size that would change a decision raises the shared effect modifier check's alarm rate from 1.3% to 4.5%
IDN-05.question: Population adjustment across a network assumes that a covariate modifies the effect of every active treatment in a class in the same way. There is one published within-network check on that assumption: fit the model with a single interaction shared across the class, refit with treatment-specific interactions one covariate at a time, and compare the posteriors and the model fit. Its authors say it likely has low power. Nobody has measured it, there is no threshold that separates a pass from a failure, and there is no statement of what a pass licenses. Scored against a known truth under a declared distribution of networks, what is it worth?
IDN-05.answer: The check does not have the resolution to test the assumption it is read as testing. Against a violation already twice the size that would change a decision, the DIC rule fires in 0.045 [0.029, 0.070] of analyses, against 0.013 [0.005, 0.029] when the assumption holds exactly: a violation that doubles the error that matters moves the alarm rate by about three percentage points. The result does not depend on where the cut is put. Scored threshold-free, the DIC difference ranks a violated network above an intact one with an AUROC of 0.557 [0.517, 0.596] at that violation, so no threshold recovers a ranking the statistic does not contain. The posterior standard deviation of the interaction contrast runs 0.30 to 1.64 against the 0.153 that would make a transported estimate materially wrong, which is why. The equivalence reading, the only one that could confirm rather than merely fail to contradict, fired zero times in 3,200 opportunities, including every replicate where the assumption held exactly; that is a statement about precision, and partly about the prior, since independent normal(0, 2.5) priors already place 0.965 of the contrast beyond the margin. Following the check is still better than not: relaxing exactly what it fires on beats relaxing everything at every target displacement and beats imposing the restriction at every displacement except zero, where the two are indistinguishable.
findings: Detection barely moves with the violation. Pooled over all eight design strata, 400 replicates each, the DIC cut at 5 fires in 0.013 [0.005, 0.029] under the global null, 0.045 [0.029, 0.070] at a contrast of 0.30 that leaves the transported estimate wrong by twice the material threshold, 0.147 at 0.60 and 0.453 at 1.20, which is eight times the decision boundary and a stress test rather than a plausible violation.

The finding survives without any threshold. Scored as a classifier, the DIC difference separates a violated network from an intact one with an AUROC of 0.557 [0.517, 0.596] at a contrast of 0.30, 0.681 [0.644, 0.718] at 0.60 and 0.843 [0.815, 0.870] at 1.20; against material error itself it reaches 0.666 at a target one standard deviation away. This analysis was prespecified, computed from the first run onward, and omitted from the first two drafts until three reviewers asked for it.

The reason is resolution. The posterior standard deviation of the difference between the two treatments' effect modifiers runs 0.30 to 1.64 on the log-odds scale across strata, against 0.153 for the difference that makes the transported estimate materially wrong. An earlier draft led with a prior-removed version of this quantity; its own sensitivity arm showed the quantity is unstable, so the measured posterior standard deviation is what is reported.

The procedure cannot give an all-clear. The equivalence reading, P(|difference| <= 0.153) > 0.95, fired in 0 of 3,200 covariate-checks, including every replicate where the two modifiers were identical by construction. This is a precision result: firing needs a posterior standard deviation below about 0.078 and the tightest stratum reaches 0.30. It is also prior-dependent in the other direction, since independent normal(0, 2.5) priors on the two coefficients put 0.965 of their contrast beyond the margin before any data are seen, above the 0.95 threshold at which the complementary margin rule fires.

The registered verdict fails, and a perfect check would have failed it too. The upper 95% bound on the probability that a passed analysis is materially wrong is 0.697, deployment- weighted, against a registered 0.10. But an oracle that knows the true interaction specification is materially wrong 0.639 of the time on the same replicates, so the check's excess over that oracle is 0.036 and is negative at small target displacements. With a threshold of 0.03 absolute risk, the estimation error of a six-study network alone exceeds it in about half of analyses when the assumption holds exactly. A threshold on total error charges a diagnostic for noise it was never built to detect.

The check is blind to what determines the harm. Its output reads only the fitted network, so its pass rate is identical at every target displacement to the last digit. Over the same fits the probability that a passed analysis is materially wrong rises from 0.427 to 0.723, an excess over the noise floor of 0.296 against a registered 0.20. The first half of that is an algebraic identity that verifies the bookkeeping; the second is empirical.

The three readings are not three procedures. The DIC rule fires without the interval rule in 0.0006 of covariate-checks and the interval rule fires without DIC in 0.106, so the DIC cut is very nearly a strict subset of the interval rule rather than a second opinion. Under the global null they differ in type I error by 0.080 on the drifting covariate and 0.087 pooling both. The 95% interval rule runs at about twice its nominal rate, 0.075 [0.046, 0.120] with no treatment-effect heterogeneity and 0.110 [0.074, 0.161] with it, so avoiding covariate selection does not deliver nominal coverage.
A fire is not a diagnosis. When a violation is present the interval rule fires on the covariate that is shared exactly in up to 0.388 of replicates.

Following the check beats the alternatives, but not uniformly, and the ranking of the alternatives is the surprise. Deployment-weighted and paired on the same replicates, relaxing exactly what fired beats relaxing everything at every displacement on both absolute and squared error, and beats imposing the restriction at displacements 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 but is indistinguishable from it at 0 (-0.00005, 95% CI [-0.00069, 0.00059]), where there is nothing to transport. Relaxing everything is worse than imposing the restriction, because the relaxed model spends precision the network does not have; it also fails its sampler diagnostics in 0.068 of replicates and 0.24 in the worst cell. Held out across design factors, the check statistic alone discriminates material error at an AUROC of 0.48 to 0.63, close to chance; adding the target displacement raises it to 0.69 to 0.83. A one-term mapping from the statistic to the probability of material error transports across network size, covariate spread and heterogeneity with absolute errors of 0.013 to 0.058, and fails across drift with an error of 0.469.

On a decision-curve basis, distrusting every adjusted analysis has higher net benefit than every rule in the panel at every action threshold from 0.05 to 0.60. This restates the noise floor rather than measuring the check: with material error present in 0.675 of passing analyses, most of it sampling noise no covariate check can predict, treat-all dominates almost regardless of what the check does.

Two software findings, against multinma 0.9.1.9002 (commit 8489bd83). The package documents class_interactions = 'exchangeable' and raises 'not yet supported', so the hierarchical relaxation this catalog entry proposed as the way forward cannot be fitted; the entry's claim that it ships in the package is wrong for this version. And under the default class_interactions = 'common', an x:.trt term in a regression formula is silently demoted to the class level, so an analyst who follows the published recipe by editing the formula alone fits the shared model twice and can never find evidence against sharing.

Two adversarial critiques before the run found nine issues between them that changed the design, and each found something the other missed. Peer review then found more, including two errors in this study's own code: contraction was divided by the standard deviation of a prior the prior-sensitivity arm was not fitted under, which inverted the reported direction of that arm's result, and the primary bound was a Wilson interval on the unweighted risk printed beside a deployment-weighted point estimate. Both were derived by reviewers from the published numbers alone, without access to the code.
IDN-05.not_answered: The design is a best case in several specific ways that favour the check, and failures attributable to those idealizations are conservative; no general lower-bound claim is made, because three features cut the other way. The true marginal reference risk in the target is supplied to the estimator. Covariates are normal with known target moments and study covariate means are drawn independently of study baselines and of the random treatment effects, so the ecological route identifying the aggregate-only treatment's interaction is unbiased by construction. IDN-05.estimand: Marginal risk difference for the aggregate-only treatment versus the individual-data treatment in a target population, with the population-average conditional log-odds effect as the mechanism scale
methods_compared: check first, then relax exactly what fired

IDN-06.title: An aggregate-only treatment's interaction is identified by assumption, by an ecological gradient or by the prior, and each fails differently
IDN-06.question: When a treatment has only aggregate data, is its effect-modifier interaction identified by the data, by the shared-interaction assumption, or by the prior, and do credible intervals cover when the assumption fails?
IDN-06.answer: By none of them reliably. With one aggregate trial the data carry no information about the treatment's interaction, yet the shared-interaction model's credible interval was as narrow as the individual-data trial's and covered 0.68 and 0.15 at discordance 0.15 and 0.3; a separate model returned its prior. With four aggregate trials the separate model covered nominally until an ecological term of 0.1 entered the between-trial gradient, then 0.71. The shared model's apparent recovery there came from the ecological bias offsetting the discordance.
findings: Direct share of posterior precision (information about the interaction itself): zero for every model with one aggregate trial.
Shared-model coverage at nonzero discordance without ecological bias: 0.149 to 0.867; separate model with a gradient: 0.942 to 0.955.
With the ecological term, separate-model bias about 0.09 and coverage 0.71 to 0.74.
IDN-06.not_answered: Conjugate normal models on contrast-level data rather than multinma fits; one covariate; fixed prior scales. Peer review has not been done.
IDN-06.design: Exact conjugate-normal calculation: an individual-data trial for one treatment, one to four aggregate trials for another at spread covariate means, discordance between the two interactions and an ecological term; shared, separate and hierarchical models.
IDN-06.estimand: Effect-modifier interaction of the aggregate-only treatment
methods_compared: separate interaction with a vague prior

IDN-07.title: Calibrating a held-out-trial falsification rule
IDN-07.question: When one trial is withheld and its contrast predicted from the rest, which pass or fail rule holds its type I error, how much power does it have, and what does omitting a variance component or mis-targeting the prediction do?
IDN-07.answer: A held-out-trial check has a controllable size if the prediction targets the withheld trial's own population and its variance includes between-trial heterogeneity: the full rule's size was 0.035 to 0.073 (registered limit 0.07, exceeded by 0.003 in one scenario). Omitting heterogeneity raised size to 0.104, and aiming the prediction at the remaining trials' population raised it to 0.96. Power against a violation as large as the effect was only 0.21 to 0.47, so a pass licenses very little.
findings: Registered verdict: FULL RULE SIZE NOT HELD, by 0.003 in one of 8 null scenarios (MCSE 0.006); every other null scenario 0.035 to 0.064.
Power of the full rule: 0.07 to 0.17 at violation 0.15 and 0.21 to 0.47 at violation 0.3.
Null mean of the discrepancy: at most 0.009 with the external target, down to -0.60 with the reduced-network target.
Sign-disagreement rule: flagged 0.02 to 0.44 of valid analyses depending on the effect's distance from zero.
IDN-07.not_answered: Continuous outcome and G-computation only; no MAIC weight variance, no Bayesian predictive or conditional-moment rule; five aggregate trials. Peer review has not been done.
IDN-07.design: One individual-data trial and five aggregate trials with a continuous outcome and linear effect modification; 24 cells crossing violation size, heterogeneity, covariate spread and withheld-trial position; full, naive, mis-targeted and decision-flip rules. 2000 replicates per cell.
IDN-07.estimand: The withheld trial's contrast in its own population, and the discrepancy between prediction and observation

IDN-09.title: A negative-control outcome for transport bias
IDN-09.question: Can a negative-control outcome detect and calibrate transport bias in an unanchored MAIC, and when does the calibration fail?
IDN-09.answer: Only in a knife-edge case. A negative-control outcome with no treatment effect detects a population difference (flag rate up to 0.83) but calibrates the primary contrast correctly only when its dependence on the unmeasured covariate equals the primary outcome's and that covariate does not modify the treatment effect (bias 0.001). Otherwise the calibrated contrast was biased by -0.18 to 0.40: it missed the modification part, overcorrected with a more strongly dependent control, and cancelled by coincidence in one scenario.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: calibrated bias -0.183 to 0.399 wherever the control's bias differed from the primary's.
Control test size 0.039 to 0.056 without a shift; power 0.04 to 0.83 with a 0.5 SD shift, rising with the control's dependence on the unmeasured covariate.
With modification by the unmeasured covariate and a matched control, calibration left 0.19 of 0.41 naive bias.
IDN-09.not_answered: One control outcome rather than a bank with empirical calibration; unanchored only; availability of control outcomes not surveyed. Peer review has not been done.
IDN-09.design: Unanchored MAIC with an unmeasured covariate shifted between populations, a negative-control outcome sharing some, all or more of its prognostic dependence, and effect modification absent or present; naive, control-test and calibrated contrasts. 16 cells, 2000 replicates each.
IDN-09.estimand: Marginal log odds ratio of the primary outcome, B versus A, in the target

IDN-10.title: A transported control-arm check carries no information about the anchored contrast
IDN-10.question: Does agreement between a MAIC-transported control arm and the target's observed control arm tell an analyst whether the anchored relative effect is biased?
IDN-10.answer: No. The check tests prognostic transport, which an anchored contrast does not need, and cannot see effect-modification transport, which it does. A prognostic shift raised the alarm rate to 0.48 while the contrast was nearly unbiased (bias -0.03 to -0.06); a modifier shift biased the log odds ratio by 0.30 with the alarm rate at 0.044. Modifier shift of 0.6 SD, no prognostic shift: alarm rate 0.044 to 0.050, contrast bias 0.28 to 0.30, coverage 0.78 to 0.82.
At every threshold on |z| the detection rate equaled the false-alarm rate (0.21 against 0.21 at 1.96); AUROC 0.502.
The check targets the right assumption only in unanchored comparisons, where the relative effect depends on prognostic transport; that case was not simulated.
IDN-10.not_answered: Binary outcome only; survival-curve and RMST versions, unanchored comparisons, offsetting prognostic mechanisms and outcome-definition or follow-up differences are not simulated. Peer review has not been done.
IDN-10.design: Anchored binary-outcome MAIC, individual data on A versus C and arm counts on B versus C; an unmeasured prognostic covariate and an unmeasured modifier of A's effect shifted independently between populations; 18 scenarios crossing both shifts and target size.
IDN-10.estimand: Anchored B-versus-A marginal log odds ratio in the target; the check's alarm as a classifier of material bias
methods_compared: transported control-arm check at several thresholds

IDN-19.title: A partition-sensitivity display for shared effect modifiers is stable exactly when every candidate partition is wrong
IDN-19.question: Does the choice of which treatments share an effect-modifier interaction move a target contrast, does the widest estimable partition fail silently, and does the range over defensible partitions contain the truth?
IDN-19.answer: No. When an aggregate-only treatment's interaction differed from both candidate classes' (by 0.3) while theirs agreed, every admissible partition returned the same answer biased by -0.30; the range over partitions was narrow (0.14), contained the truth in 5% of replicates, and the only available fit test rejected at its nominal 5%. The widest partition covered 0.37. The range widened and contained the correct partition only when the candidate classes disagreed with each other.
findings: Widest partition bias -0.30 and coverage 0.37 at the primary cell, with the fit test rejecting in 5% of analyses.
The fit test detects disagreement between treatments with identified interactions (41% when C differs from B) and never the aggregate-only treatment's own departure.
With the candidate classes disagreeing, {B}{CD} or {BD}{C} was unbiased when D truly shared that class's interaction.
IDN-19.not_answered: Small hand-built network, continuous outcome, linear modification, three partitions, sufficient statistics drawn directly; no overlap factor or ML-NMR fits. Peer review has not been done.
IDN-19.design: A network with individual data on A vs B and aggregate trials of A vs C and A vs D; interaction heterogeneity within and between classes; three admissible partitions fitted by generalized least squares. 6 cells, 4000 replicates each.
IDN-19.estimand: D versus A mean difference at the target covariate mean
methods_compared: network fits under three admissible shared-modifier partitions

MIS-01.title: Missing covariate values in the individual-data trial of a MAIC
MIS-01.question: When a matched covariate is missing for some patients in the individual-data trial, when is complete-case MAIC biased, and do inverse-probability-of-observation weighting and multiple imputation repair it?
MIS-01.answer: Complete-case MAIC bias is set by the missingness mechanism, not the rate. It is unbiased when missingness depends only on matched covariates, including the missing covariate itself, and biased already at 15% missingness when it depends on an unmatched effect modifier, the outcome with modification, or an unmatched covariate in one arm only. Weighting and imputation repair the missing-at-random cases (imputation with arm interactions most reliably) but are biased by up to 0.22 when missingness depends on the missing covariate itself, where complete case is not.

Missingness in one arm driven by an unmatched prognostic covariate: complete-case bias -0.34 at 15% and -0.65 at 30%, with no effect modification.
Missingness driven by the missing covariate: complete case within 0.035; observation weighting and imputation biased by up to 0.22.
Imputation without arm interactions carried small systematic bias (up to 0.05); observation weighting failed with extreme weights when 60% to 95% of one arm was missing.
MIS-01.not_answered: Missing outcomes, binary outcomes, STC, overlap levels and pattern-mixture sensitivity analysis not run; single-driver mechanisms only. Peer review has not been done.
MIS-01.design: Continuous-outcome MAIC with one partly missing matched covariate, one observed matched covariate and one unmatched covariate; 36 cells crossing missingness rate, six mechanisms and whether the unmatched covariate modifies the effect; complete case, observation weighting and congenial or generic imputation. 1000 replicates per cell.
MIS-01.estimand: Target-population mean difference, A versus C, in the anchored MAIC

MIS-02.title: Participation weights multiplied by censoring weights under heavy censoring and poor overlap
MIS-02.question: Does the TADA estimator, participation weights times inverse-probability-of-censoring weights with bootstrap variance, stay unbiased and well calibrated when censoring is heavy, overlap poor and the two weight sets correlated?
MIS-02.design: Transported RMST difference from a two-arm trial with covariate-dependent censoring; 25% or 60% censoring, good or poor overlap, positively or negatively correlated weight sets, plus two null controls; participation-only Kaplan-Meier, TADA with bootstrap and fixed-weight sandwich SE, TADA with a misspecified censoring model. 10 cells, 500 replicates each.

MIS-03.title: What conditioning on sampled target moments costs
MIS-03.question: Population adjustment treats a target trial's published covariate means and standard deviations as exact, though they are sample estimates. By how much does that cost interval coverage at realistic sample sizes, and what would a publication have to report for a correction to work?
MIS-03.answer: Two things, established by different means. Analytically: the variance a standard interval omits is (1-2k)Var_T(tau)/n_T to first order, where k is how far the target trial's own treatment effect is modified by the same covariates as the source trial's, so the sign is set by a quantity the usual inputs do not identify; and a correction adding only the positive term is closer to the right variance than doing nothing only when k < 1/4. Empirically, and only in an exploratory subset: the omission runs from 9.5% too much variance to 14.9% too little and moves coverage between 92.1% and 96.2%. The registered analysis is uninformative and the confirmatory coverage question remains open.
findings: The prespecified analysis returned uninformative. Its gates require the reference interval and the negative controls to be nominal, and at poor overlap the Wald sandwich undercovers by up to 7 points for every method including scenarios with no effect modification at all, where the population omission is exactly zero. That is a source-variance failure, not a target-moment one.

The sign of the omission is an analytic identity, not a simulation finding: (1-2k)Var_T(tau)/n_T. Regressing the measured omission on it across all 216 scenarios with effect modification gives a slope of 1.003 (SE 0.042). An earlier draft claimed the simulation located the cancellation point; peer review corrected that and the claim was retracted.

The two corrections an analyst can deploy add only the positive term and omit the cross-covariance. They beat doing nothing only when k < 1/4, and are worse than doing nothing between 1/4 and 1/2. The design has no interior k with which to test this, so no recommendation is made for intermediate alignment. A draft claim that they help whenever k < 1/2 was wrong and was corrected in review.

In the exploratory subset the status quo was the only method to leave 93% to 97% coverage, and it left in both directions. Magnitude tracks the ratio of source to target information, so a large source trial matched to a small target publication is the worst case, not a small target trial.
Peer review left a standing recommendation of major revision. The confirmatory question needs a fresh registered run with an ex ante overlap restriction or a validated source variance estimator.
MIS-03.not_answered: The registered coverage question is not confirmatorily answered: every usable coverage result comes from a post-run restriction conditioning on an observed outcome. One estimator, one outcome type, one information structure. Covariates are multivariate normal, which is also the assumption the deployable correction is derived under, so it is measured under conditions favorable to it; skewed, bounded and categorical covariates are untested. The outcome is continuous and the effect additive, so marginal and conditional effects coincide, and nothing transfers directly to binary or time-to-event outcomes, where MAIC is most used. Effect modification lies exactly in the span of the matched moments, so this is a variance result under correct identification and says nothing about bias. The target moments and the target treatment effect come from the same trial, which is the common case but not the only one. STC, ML-NMR, ML-UMR and NMI have different sensitivities and are not covered. EST-07's other components, model uncertainty in reconstructed correlations, inclusion-criteria ambiguity and secular drift, are not sampling error and are untouched. The alignment parameter imposes exact non-negative proportionality between source and target modifier coefficients, so modifier sets differing in direction or overlapping only partially are untested.
MIS-03.design: Anchored MAIC on a continuous outcome, with the target trial's participants generated and then discarded so the estimator sees only a published baseline table. 252 scenarios crossing source size, target size, overlap, effect-modification strength calibrated to a fixed target-population standard deviation, the alignment between the two trials' effect modification, and whether the analyst's borrowed correlation is correct.

MIS-04.title: Choosing among population-adjustment models on the same data
MIS-04.question: When the adjustment model is chosen from the analyzed data, does the chosen model's interval keep its coverage, and what does averaging over candidates change?

MOD-02.title: Flexible outcome models reduced but did not remove transport bias where the target left the data, and could not see a modification they were not built to see
MOD-02.question: Do flexible outcome models remove the transport bias a parametric STC incurs under threshold, hinge and covariate-interaction surfaces, and with valid intervals, as overlap worsens?
MOD-02.answer: Largely yes, the refuting sentence holds. Under a hinge in the treatment effect at a target 1.5 SD from the source, parametric STC was biased by -0.144 and a GAM with smooth treatment modification by -0.085 (coverage 0.93): about 40% less bias, short of the registered halving, with the same RMSE (0.314 against 0.318) because its variance was larger. Under a covariate-by-covariate modification every method was biased by about -0.18, since additive smooths cannot represent a product. A threshold prognostic term largely cancelled in all methods.
findings: Bias grew with target distance for every method on the hinge and product surfaces.
The structured GAM (smooth prognosis, linear modification) was no better than STC on the hinge surface.
Coverage stayed near 0.90 to 0.93 in biased cells because intervals were wide (empirical SD about 0.3).
