MOD-15.title: The half-standard-error pooling rule for interactions is stated in the wrong standard error
MOD-15.question: The published rule pools within-trial and across-trial interaction estimates when they differ by less than half the across-trial standard error. What are its pass rate, the bias and coverage of what it reports, and how does it compare with a test stated in the difference's own standard error?
MOD-15.answer: The difference's standard error is sqrt(sW^2 + sA^2), not sA, so under equality the rule pools with probability at most 0.383 (0.31 to 0.37 in the networks studied): it refuses valid pooling most of the time in every regime. When it pools under ecological bias, the pooled interval can cover as little as 22%. Its RMSE matches never pooling to within 0.3%, forgoing the 2% to 19% gain pooling offers when the estimates agree.
findings: Pass probability under equality: 0.314 to 0.374, bounded above by P(|Z| < 0.5) = 0.383 in any network.

Coverage of the pooled interval given pooling falls with ecological bias: 0.72 at delta 0.1 and 0.22 at delta 0.2 with 20 trials and dispersed trial means, where the rule still pools in 6% and 0.04% of analyses.
Averaged over its decisions, the rule's RMSE is within 0.3% of never pooling in every configuration.
Never pooling had the lowest worst-case RMSE over ecological bias 0 to 0.2 in five of six configurations; always pooling had it in one.
An individual-level check of 2000 networks per configuration reproduced the standard errors, the pass probability (0.366 against 0.374 exact) and the conditional coverage (0.951 against 0.950).
MOD-15.not_answered: Independent normal estimates with known standard errors; no between-trial heterogeneity; all trials with individual data. The ML-NMR case, where aggregate trials inform only the across-trial component, is not computed. No agreement rule can detect trial-level confounding that is small relative to the across-trial standard error. Peer review has not been done.
MOD-15.design: Exact bivariate-normal computation of pass probability, bias, RMSE and coverage for never pooling, always pooling, the half-SE rule and tests on the difference at 5% and 20%, over 24 configurations: 5, 10 or 20 trials of 200, trial covariate means spread with SD 0.25 or 0.75, ecological bias 0 to 0.4.
MOD-15.n_sim: Exact computation; individual-level check of 2000 networks in each of four configurations

MOD-16.title: Arm-separate matching cancels the aggregate trial's chance imbalance; pooled matching carries it
MOD-16.question: Arm-separate matching weights each individual-data arm to the corresponding aggregate arm; pooled matching uses one weight function. When does each give a biased anchored comparison, and is the bias of arm-separate matching the product of unmatched prognostic strength and aggregate arm imbalance, as the design claims?
MOD-16.answer: The product claim is wrong. Given an aggregate-trial imbalance kappa, pooled matching is biased by kappa (beta/2 + gamma_X + gamma_U rho_T) and arm-separate matching by kappa gamma_U (rho_T - rho_S); simulation matched both (slopes 1.00 and 0.96). Arm-separate matching reproduces the aggregate imbalance in the individual-data contrast so it cancels, and is biased only when an unmatched prognostic covariate relates to the matched one differently in the two trials. It had smaller bias than pooled matching in every scenario with an imposed imbalance and 10% to 27% lower RMSE under chance imbalance.
findings: With the matched-unmatched correlation shared between trials, arm-separate bias was within Monte Carlo error of zero in all 16 scenarios with an unmatched prognostic covariate and an imposed imbalance (largest 0.011).
Slope of simulated on predicted bias: pooled 1.004 (SE 0.011); arm-separate 0.958 (SE 0.035).
Under chance imbalance, arm-separate RMSE over pooled 0.73 to 0.90; its sandwich interval overcovered (0.965 to 0.991) because the two trials' imbalances are positively correlated.
Two-stage MAIC behaved like pooled matching, correcting the individual trial's imbalance but not the aggregate trial's.
The design's candidate diagnostic, the weighted difference in the unmatched covariate between arms, estimates rho_S kappa and cannot see rho_T; its correlation with arm-separate bias was -0.41.
MOD-16.not_answered: Continuous outcome, linear model, one matched and one unmatched covariate, shared effect modification; the non-collapsible case, where arm-separate matching compares arms in different populations, is not studied, and the arm-separate interval's conservatism is not repaired. Peer review has not been done.
MOD-16.design: Anchored MAIC with a continuous outcome, 300 per arm; 96 scenarios crossing an imposed aggregate-arm imbalance in the matched covariate (0, 0.1, 0.2 SD or chance), the unmatched covariate's prognostic strength, the matched-unmatched correlation in each trial and shared effect modification; unadjusted, pooled, arm-separate and two-stage MAIC.
MOD-16.estimand: Anchored B-versus-A mean difference in the target

MOD-18.title: An estimated risk score used as a regressor
MOD-18.question: When a risk score estimated in a prognostic cohort is used as a regressor for treatment-effect heterogeneity, does treating it as data understate the interval, and is the understatement worst at the tails of risk?
MOD-18.answer: Little, given a prognostic cohort of about a thousand patients or more: propagating the score's estimation uncertainty widened intervals by at most 2.4%, and plug-in coverage stayed near nominal. With 300 cohort patients the widening reached 7% at the risk tails against about 1% at the median, confirming that the understatement is worst where recommendations are made, and plug-in coverage fell to 0.924. The registered rule (plug-in coverage at least 0.93 everywhere) was missed in that one scenario, so the refuting sentence fails as registered.
findings: Widening ratio 1.001 to 1.024 with cohorts of 1000 or 5000; 1.011 to 1.073 with 300.
Tails against median with 300: widening 1.065 to 1.073 against 1.011 to 1.012.
Plug-in coverage 0.924 to 0.970; propagated 0.932 to 0.974.
MOD-18.not_answered: Pairwise six-trial analysis; frequentist bootstrap rather than a joint or cut Bayesian model; well-specified score. Peer review has not been done.
MOD-18.design: Logistic prognostic score from cohorts of 300 to 5000, used in a six-trial individual-data meta-regression with calibration drift; plug-in and bootstrap-propagated intervals for the treatment effect at the 10th, 50th and 90th risk percentiles. 6 cells, 500 replicates each.
MOD-18.n_sim: 500 per scenario, 3,000 in total, each with 20 bootstrap refits
MOD-18.estimand: Treatment log odds ratio at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles of true risk
methods_compared: plug-in interval treating the score as data
interval adding bootstrap variance of the score

OUT-02.title: Effective sample size counted in events: right direction, no gain over ESS times the event rate
OUT-02.question: With rare binary outcomes, does an effective sample size counted in events (EESS) predict when a MAIC interval fails better than the reported ESS multiplied by the event rate, and in which direction do the two diverge?
OUT-02.answer: EESS is the reciprocal of the sandwich variance of a weighted log odds, and it differs from ESS times the event rate by E_w[w]E_w[p]/E_w[wp]: below 1 when weights concentrate on high-risk patients, above 1 on low-risk ones (the design had the direction reversed). As a predictor of failure the two were equivalent (AUROC 0.839 and 0.858) and ESS alone was poor (0.662). Their predictive value comes from zero-event analyses; once an estimate exists, non-coverage is near nominal and neither predicts it.
findings: Median EESS / (ESS p): 0.47 to 0.79 when weights concentrate on high-risk patients, 1.28 to 2.40 on low-risk patients, 1.00 to 1.03 when the shift is in a non-prognostic covariate.
AUROC for failure (no estimate or non-coverage) over 108,000 analyses: EESS 0.839, ESS x event rate 0.858, ESS 0.662; the registered rule, requiring EESS to be better by 0.05, is refuted.
No estimate (an arm with no events) in up to 86% of analyses at risk 0.005 and 300 per arm.
Among analyses with an estimate, non-coverage was 5.7% and the diagnostics' AUROC 0.54 to 0.59 (exploratory).
OUT-02.not_answered: One prognostic covariate, MAIC on means; the penalized, Firth, Bayesian and fail-closed estimators were not run, and unanchored comparisons and multivariable separation are outside the design. Peer review has not been done.
OUT-02.design: Binary-outcome MAIC with one prognostic covariate among three, 108 scenarios crossing event risk (0.005 to 0.1), size and direction of the target shift relative to risk, sample size and effect; EESS, ESS times the event rate and ESS as per-analysis predictors of failure.
OUT-02.estimand: Target-population marginal log odds ratio, A versus C; failure of its interval

OUT-05.title: The transported mean is safe and the responder probability is not
OUT-05.question: When a bounded continuous outcome is transported by G-computation with a pooled normal residual, is the mean contrast safe while the responder-probability contrast is biased, and does a floor make the bias depend on the target population?
OUT-05.answer: Yes. With a pooled normal residual the transported mean contrast was unbiased while the responder-probability contrast was biased by up to 0.10 when the arms' dispersions differed, with opposite signs at a threshold near the median and one in the tail. Arm-specific SDs fixed it only for normal errors without a floor; Tobit fixed the floor but not skew; logistic regression of the responder indicator was unbiased everywhere. A floor biased the mean contrast by under 2% of the effect, somewhat more at the larger target shift.
findings: Dissociation confirmed: pooled-SD mean contrast within 3 MCSE without a floor; responder bias up to 0.102 at SD ratio 2.
Normal model with arm-specific SDs: responder bias up to 0.058 with a floor and 0.070 with skew.
Tobit: at most 0.003 with normal errors, 0.040 with skew; logistic responder model: at most 0.006 in every scenario.
Floor of 25%: linear mean-contrast bias -0.012 to 0.010 at shift 0.3 and -0.070 to 0.038 at shift 1.
OUT-05.not_answered: One source trial, no ceiling, no intervals, no ML-NMR. Peer review has not been done.
OUT-05.design: Source trial with arm-specific residual SDs, skewed or normal errors and a floor at 0, 10% or 25% mass, transported to targets at two shifts; normal pooled-SD, arm-specific SD, Tobit and direct logistic responder models; mean and responder contrasts at two thresholds. 24 cells, 1000 replicates each.
OUT-05.estimand: Target mean difference and target responder-probability differences at two thresholds
methods_compared: logistic regression of the responder indicator

OUT-06.title: Change scores and endpoints do not diverge under population adjustment
OUT-06.question: When baseline severity modifies the treatment effect, do change-score and endpoint analyses give different target-population contrasts after population adjustment, in proportion to the product of the interaction and the baseline shift?
OUT-06.answer: No. Baseline is pre-treatment, so the target follow-up and change contrasts are one quantity under any adjustment. Across 24 scenarios, MAIC and G-computation never diverged beyond Monte Carlo error, and were identical to machine precision in unanchored comparisons. The only divergence was in naive unanchored comparisons, equal to 1.00 times the baseline shift and independent of the baseline-by-treatment interaction.
findings: Adjusted estimators: largest mean endpoint-minus-change difference 0.0068, within 3 Monte Carlo SE of zero in every scenario; in unanchored comparisons the per-replicate difference was at most 4e-13.
Naive unanchored comparisons: difference = 1.001 (SE 0.002) x shift + 0.007 (SE 0.007) x interaction x shift. Endpoint bias is (b + beta) shift and change bias (b + beta - 1) shift.
Naive anchored comparisons agree in expectation across representations but are both biased by the unadjusted modification.

The design's proposed product structure was derived from a misreading: with baseline as a covariate, the treatment and treatment-by-baseline coefficients of a linear model are identical for follow-up and change.
OUT-06.not_answered: Continuous outcome with a linear conditional mean only; nonlinear links, threshold-based responder estimands and joint repeated-measures models are not tested. Peer review has not been done.
OUT-06.design: Anchored and unanchored comparisons, individual data on A versus C and arm means on B versus C, 24 scenarios crossing baseline shift (0, 0.5, 1 SD), baseline-by-treatment interaction (0, 0.3) and baseline-to-follow-up correlation (0.4, 0.8), 300 per arm.
OUT-06.estimand: Target-population mean difference in follow-up, B versus A
methods_compared: each in endpoint and change representation

OUT-07.title: Informative censoring on the two sides of an indirect comparison
OUT-07.question: When censoring depends on latent risk in the source and comparator trials to different degrees, does the bias cancel in the indirect RMST contrast, what does source-side IPCW achieve, and does a one-sided comparator sensitivity analysis cover the truth?
OUT-07.answer: Informative censoring cancels in an indirect RMST contrast only when the two mechanisms match. Unanchored, with differing mechanisms the bias was -2.3 to +1.4 months against a true difference of 0.62, reversing the comparison in up to 97% of analyses; equal mechanisms nearly cancelled. Anchored comparisons were protected (bias within 0.22) because both arms of each trial shared its mechanism. Adjusting only the source by inverse probability of censoring weighting helped partly where only the source was informative and broke the cancellation where both were.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: unanchored bias -2.326 to 1.416 months when mechanisms differed; -0.080 to 0.021 when equal.
Anchored: bias -0.202 to 0.219 months in all 12 scenarios.
Source-side IPCW with a proxy correlated 0.7 with latent risk: 1.42 to 0.99 months where only the source was informative; -0.08 to -0.52 where both were equally informative.
The comparator delta reproducing the truth lay outside 0.5 to 2 in up to 70% of analyses (median 2.4 with strong dependence at 50% censoring).
OUT-07.not_answered: No covariate shift between trials; time-constant censoring hazards; one sensitivity parameterization; one baseline proxy. Peer review has not been done.
OUT-07.design: Shared-frailty event and censoring processes with separate dependence in the source and comparator; 24 cells crossing the two dependences, censoring prevalence and anchored or unanchored design; naive Kaplan-Meier, source-side IPCW and a comparator delta-adjusted sensitivity analysis. 1000 replicates per cell.
OUT-07.estimand: RMST difference at 24 months, unanchored (A minus B) or anchored ((A minus C) minus (B minus C))
methods_compared: source-side inverse probability of censoring weighting

OUT-08.title: Overdispersed and zero-inflated counts transported by G-computation
OUT-08.question: For count outcomes transported to a target, does overdispersion bias the estimate or only its interval, and when the fraction of structural zeros differs between populations, what does a count model transport wrongly and what repairs it?
OUT-08.answer: Overdispersion leaves the transported rate ratio unbiased and makes the Poisson interval too narrow (coverage down to 0.61); a sandwich or negative binomial restores it. A structural-zero fraction that differs between source and target biases the transported absolute rate in every count model, including zero-inflated Poisson, by up to 0.56 on the log scale; the rate ratio is protected only without effect modification. Recalibrating the zero part to the target's reported zero proportion repairs the absolute rate when the source has structural zeros to learn from.
findings: Poisson rate-ratio coverage 0.846 to 0.610 under overdispersion with bias at most 0.010; sandwich 0.926 to 0.948, so the registered rule (0.93 everywhere) was missed by 0.004 in one cell with MCSE 0.012.
Differing structural-zero fractions: absolute log-rate bias 0.40 to 0.56 in absolute value for Poisson, negative binomial and zero-inflated Poisson, coverage 0.000 to 0.028.
Rate ratio with differing zero fractions: bias at most 0.007 without effect modification, up to 0.11 with it.
Zero part recalibrated to the target's zero proportion: absolute-rate bias at most 0.04 when the source had structural zeros, 0.25 when it had none.
OUT-08.not_answered: One covariate; frailty, exposure weighting, recurrent events and zero-inflated negative binomial not run. Peer review has not been done.
OUT-08.design: G-computation from an individual-data trial with negative-binomial or zero-inflated Poisson counts, 14 cells separating dispersion from structural-zero differences, with and without effect modification; Poisson, sandwich, negative binomial, zero-inflated and recalibrated zero-inflated fits. 500 replicates per cell.
OUT-08.estimand: Log rate ratio, A versus C, and log rate under A, in the target population
methods_compared: zero-inflated Poisson with recalibrated zero part

OUT-10.title: A proportional-odds violation biases an expected-utility difference in both directions, depending on where the utility increments sit
OUT-10.question: Does a proportional-odds violation bias a target-standardized expected-utility difference in proportion to the utility increments at the violated cut-point, and does relaxing proportional odds remove it?
OUT-10.answer: Not as predicted. A proportional-odds violation biased the target-standardized expected-utility difference whichever end carried the utility increments: by -0.025 and -0.047 with the increments at the violated cut-point and by +0.026 and +0.024 at the other end, with coverage 0.67 to 0.85. The single coefficient understates the effect at the violated cut-point and overstates it elsewhere. Separate cut-point logistic models were unbiased with coverage 0.93 to 0.98 in every cell.
findings: Registered primary (aligned bias at least twice misaligned) not confirmed: misaligned bias was of similar size and opposite sign.
Under proportional odds both models were unbiased with nominal coverage (null control passed).
Relaxing proportional odds cost little precision: RMSE 0.022 to 0.032 versus 0.023 to 0.056.
OUT-10.not_answered: One individual-data trial rather than an ML-NMR network; separate cut-point regressions as the relaxed model; fixed utilities; no dichotomized-publication arm. Peer review has not been done.
OUT-10.design: Four-category ordinal outcome with proportional odds or a violation at the bottom or top cut-point; utilities with increments at the bottom or top; proportional-odds and separate cut-point logistic regressions standardized over a shifted target. 3 cells, 400 replicates each.
OUT-10.n_sim: 400 per cell, 3 cells, two utility vectors each
OUT-10.estimand: Target-standardized expected-utility difference, A minus C

OUT-13.title: Is a reconstruction ensemble's spread the reconstruction error?
OUT-13.question: When individual data are reconstructed repeatedly from a published Kaplan-Meier curve, does the spread of the ensemble match the true reconstruction error, so that pooling it like multiple imputation is valid?
OUT-13.design: Simulated trial data rendered as a pixel-rounded Kaplan-Meier figure with or without a risk table, reconstructed by Guyot's algorithm; analyst-variant and observation-model ensembles scored by the ratio of their spread to the true reconstruction error for RMST, milestone and extrapolated survival. 13 cells, 300 replicates each.

OUT-14.title: Assessment grids that differ between trials
OUT-14.question: When two trials assess progression on different visit schedules, how much does treating recorded event times as exact bias a transported RMST difference, and do midpoint imputation or an interval-censored model remove it?
OUT-14.answer: Treating visit-recorded event times as exact biases a cross-trial RMST difference by half the spacing times the event probability by the horizon, with the sign set by which trial visits less often. A 3-month difference in spacing produced a spurious difference of 1.4 months with no true effect, and removed 1.0 of a true 1.2 months in another scenario. Moving events to the interval midpoint or fitting an interval-censored model reduced the bias below 0.1 month.
findings: Naive bias on the prediction (d_B/2)F_B(tau) - (d_A/2)F_A(tau): slope 1.014 (SE 0.005) over 32 scenarios.
Where the schedules differed by 2 months or more, naive bias was 0.94 to 1.43 months in absolute value; materiality confirmed in all 16 such scenarios.
Midpoint shift: largest bias 0.081 months; interval-censored Weibull: 0.071 months.

The registered control (equal schedules, zero bias) failed in 2 of 8 cells, both where the arms' event probabilities differed; there the bias matched the mechanism's prediction (-0.14 and -0.14 against -0.14 and -0.11).
OUT-14.not_answered: Binary event-by-time endpoints, different maximum follow-up, reconstruction error from digitized curves and visit-window jitter were not simulated. Peer review has not been done.
OUT-14.design: Unanchored comparison of two single arms with Weibull event times, 32 cells crossing each trial's assessment spacing (0 to 3 months), the event rate and the true difference; naive, midpoint and interval-censored analyses of RMST at 24 months. 1000 replicates per cell.
OUT-14.estimand: Difference in restricted mean survival time at 24 months, B minus A

OVL-01.title: Unsupported target mass matters only where the effect is modified
OVL-01.question: When part of the target population lies outside the source trial's support, do weight and covariate diagnostics identify the analyses that fail, or is the modification in the unsupported region, which they cannot see, what decides it?
OVL-01.answer: Unsupported target mass caused bias only where the effect bent in the unsupported direction (up to 0.29 for G-computation and 0.30 for MAIC with 27% of the target unsupported), and none with linear modification or orthogonal alignment. Weight and covariate diagnostics, identical across those scenarios by construction, discriminated failed analyses at chance within an overlap level (AUROC 0.48 to 0.52). An outcome-informed score reached 0.59 to 0.66, missing the registered margin by 0.01; neither was usable. Trimming to the supported region was unbiased for the restricted estimand.
findings: Registered verdict NEITHER USABLE: at the largest unsupported mass, alignment-aware score minus Kish ESS AUROC 0.090 (SE 0.013) against a 0.10 margin, both below 0.7.
Bias with full alignment and bent modification: -0.29 (G-computation) and -0.30 (MAIC); orthogonal alignment at most 0.023; linear modification at most 0.017 at every truncation.
Kish ESS, unsupported mass and largest weight share: AUROC 0.48 to 0.52 within each overlap level.
Trimmed G-computation against the restricted estimand: bias at most 0.026, coverage 0.926 to 0.962.
OVL-01.not_answered: Continuous outcome, two covariates; ML-NMR, ML-UMR and NMI not run; failure defined by non-coverage. Peer review has not been done.
OVL-01.design: Anchored transport with one covariate truncated in the source; 36 cells crossing unsupported mass, whether the unsupported direction modifies the effect, linear or bent modification and its strength; MAIC, spline G-computation and trimmed G-computation; weight diagnostics and an outcome-informed score scored as classifiers of failure. 1000 replicates per cell.
OVL-01.estimand: Target mean difference over the whole target law; restricted estimand over the supported region
methods_compared: G-computation trimmed to the observed range
Kish ESS, unsupported mass, largest weight share and an outcome-informed alignment score as diagnostics

OVL-02.title: An infeasible MAIC is signaled by its own balance table, not by its effective sample size
OVL-02.question: MAIC has no solution when the target mean lies outside the convex hull of the source covariates. Does the optimizer say so, and can ESS, the maximum weight or the residual balance tell infeasible analyses from hard feasible ones?
OVL-02.answer: The residual imbalance of the returned weights does, almost perfectly: above 0.001 in 99.9% of infeasible and 0.1% of feasible analyses. The optimizer reported convergence on 17% of infeasible problems. ESS ranks analyses well but the conventional rule of ESS below 10% of n flagged 73% of feasible analyses near the hull boundary as well as every infeasible one, so it cannot separate impossible from hard; and hard feasible analyses near the boundary undercovered badly anyway.
findings: AUROC for infeasibility: residual imbalance 1.000, ESS 0.996, maximum weight 0.993, optimizer non-convergence 0.909.
ESS below 10% of n: flags 100% of infeasible and 73% of feasible analyses in the near-boundary scenarios.
Silent failure: the optimizer reported convergence on 0% to 8% of infeasible problems with 3 covariates and 22% to 34% with 8.
Infeasible analyses had ESS about 1 and no usable estimate; feasible analyses near the boundary had ESS 3 to 14 and coverage 0.62 to 0.85.
OVL-02.not_answered: Only feasibility of the mean constraint; support for the target joint law cannot be checked from published marginals. Normal covariates, MAIC on means, one sample size; the proposed diagnostics' computability taxonomy was not simulated. Peer review has not been done.
OVL-02.design: Binary-outcome MAIC with 3 or 8 covariates and a target shifted so 0% to 90% of source samples were infeasible by linear program, with and without effect modification; 24 scenarios; ESS, maximum weight, residual imbalance and convergence code scored as detectors of infeasibility.
OVL-02.estimand: Linear-program feasibility of the calibration, and the target marginal log odds ratio
methods_compared: residual imbalance of the returned weights

OVL-06.title: Planning a MAIC from the estimator's influence function, not from n or Kish ESS
OVL-06.question: Before any data exist, which planning quantity predicts the precision a MAIC will achieve: nominal sample size, Kish effective sample size, or the estimator's influence-function variance evaluated at posited source and target laws?
OVL-06.answer: The influence-function variance. It predicted the achieved SD within 10% in 85% of 72 scenarios, missing only at 150 patients with 10% prevalence. Kish ESS was within 10% in 58% and understated the achieved SD in 99% of scenarios, so it is optimistic, not the conservative quantity it is usually taken to be; nominal n was within 10% in 21%.
findings: Planned SE over achieved SD, median (range): influence function 0.963 (0.827 to 1.023); Kish ESS 0.912 (0.745 to 1.004); nominal n 0.797 (0.541 to 0.985).
Kish ESS understated the achieved SD in 99% of scenarios; its error grew with the target shift.
All 11 influence-function misses were at 150 patients and 10% prevalence; its median ratio was 0.908 at 150 patients and 0.981 at 1000.
The refuting sentence, that nominal n with an overlap adjustment is good enough, fails its registered criterion (58% of scenarios within 10% against the 90% required).
OVL-06.not_answered: The planner is assumed to know the source and target laws. Binary outcome, anchored-side precision and MAIC on means only; the unanchored bias floor and survival outcomes are not run. Peer review has not been done.
OVL-06.design: Binary-outcome MAIC with 2 or 5 covariates, 72 scenarios crossing total size (150, 400, 1000), target shift, dimension, allocation and prevalence; three planned SEs computed from the posited laws compared with the SD achieved over replicates.
OVL-06.estimand: SD of the MAIC estimate of the target marginal log odds ratio

QBA-06.title: A misclassified covariate that is both balanced and a modifier
QBA-06.question: When a binary effect modifier is misclassified in the source, the target or both, which corrections does population adjustment need, and is correcting the outcome model alone enough?
QBA-06.answer: No. MAIC on a misclassified binary modifier was biased even with identical assays in both studies (-0.03 to -0.13 on the log odds ratio scale), because reweighting recorded categories leaves each category's true composition at the source's; correcting the target prevalence alone did not help. Correcting only STC's outcome model left bias of -0.012 to -0.051. Fully corrected STC and MAIC with weights chosen on the latent prevalence were unbiased (within 0.006).
findings: Refuting sentence fails: outcome-only correction biased beyond 3 MCSE and 0.03 in some scenarios (to -0.051).
MAIC on the recorded covariate with identical assays: bias beyond 3 MCSE in 4 of 4 scenarios.
Latent-prevalence MAIC and fully corrected STC: bias -0.006 to 0.006.
QBA-06.not_answered: Known assay parameters; one binary covariate; no interval assessment. Peer review has not been done.
QBA-06.design: Anchored transport with a misclassified binary modifier under four assay scenarios and two modification strengths; naive, prevalence-corrected and latent-weight MAIC; naive, outcome-only corrected and fully corrected latent-class STC. 8 cells, 1000 replicates each.
QBA-06.estimand: Marginal log odds ratio, A versus C, in the target's true covariate law
methods_compared: STC with the outcome model corrected

QBA-07.title: Outcome ascertainment in an external comparator
QBA-07.question: Does an interval-censored analysis cover the ascertainment differences between a trial and a routine-care comparator, or do missed detections and risk-dependent visiting still bias the RMST contrast?
QBA-07.answer: Partly. With every progression detected, an interval-censored model removed the bias from the external arm's sparser visits (within 0.05 months) and was not biased by visits that depended on patients' risk at the strength simulated. When the external arm missed progression at some visits, every method was biased, by 0.25 to 0.38 months at a per-visit sensitivity of 0.85 and 0.67 to 0.94 at 0.7, against a true difference of 1.59 months. Missed detection needs its own bias parameter.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: interval-censored bias 0.25 to 0.94 months with missed detections.
Perfect detection: interval-censored bias -0.05 to 0.01 months; recorded times up to 0.42.
Risk-dependent visiting reduced the recorded-time bias and left the interval-censored model unbiased, contrary to DESIGN.md's prediction.
QBA-07.not_answered: No lag, linkage loss or false positives; one frailty and visiting strength; no sensitivity analysis over the detection parameter; no population adjustment. Peer review has not been done.
QBA-07.design: Trial arm with scheduled visits against an external arm with regular or risk-dependent visits and per-visit detection sensitivity of 1, 0.85 or 0.7; Kaplan-Meier, midpoint and interval-censored Weibull RMST. 12 cells, 1000 replicates each.
QBA-07.estimand: RMST at 24 months, external arm B minus trial arm A, from true event times

QBA-11.title: Which failures double robustness covers
QBA-11.question: Does a doubly robust MAIC protect against an omitted confounder, and what happens to a sensitivity grid built on a misspecified outcome model?
QBA-11.answer: Double robustness protects against one misspecified nuisance model and nothing else. With an omitted confounder the augmented estimator carried exactly the same bias as correctly specified weighting or outcome-regression estimators, and with both models wrong the misspecification and omitted-variable biases added. A sensitivity grid built on a misspecified analysis is therefore shifted by the misspecification bias. With exact-balance weights, augmentation by an outcome model built from the balanced terms reproduces MAIC.
findings: Both models correct: augmented bias equal to the omitted-variable bias in all 16 scenarios; largest difference from correct outcome regression 0.0015.
Omitted variable absent, one model wrong: augmented estimator unbiased (second null control held); the wrong single-model estimator biased by up to 0.20.
Both models wrong: bias additive in misspecification and omitted-variable parts, largest interaction 0.008, within 3 MCSE in 16 of 16 scenarios.

Registered region-inclusion criterion not met as stated (0.888 against a 0.90 threshold) because the region omitted sampling error; the misspecified region was displaced by 0.195 to 0.201 at every omitted-variable strength.
QBA-11.not_answered: Continuous outcome only; no cross-fitting; drMAIC E-value screen and a formally bias-indexed doubly robust estimator not run. Peer review has not been done.
QBA-11.design: Unanchored transport with a nonlinear outcome, misspecifiable weighting and outcome models and an omitted binary confounder; MAIC, outcome regression and augmented estimators under every combination of model correctness; 16 cells crossing omitted-variable strength, imbalance and overlap. 2000 replicates per cell.
methods_compared: MAIC with correct or wrong weights
outcome regression with correct or wrong model
augmented (doubly robust) estimator under the four combinations

QBA-13.title: A simulated-covariate bias analysis by STC and by MAIC
QBA-13.question: Is a MAIC version of the simulated-covariate bias analysis infeasible or too imprecise, as its authors assumed when restricting it to STC?
QBA-13.answer: The MAIC extension of the simulated-covariate bias analysis was feasible in at least 99.8% of replicates across assumed target prevalences from 0.1 to 0.9, lost effective sample size to 85 to 109 of 300 only at the extreme, and had a reported SE 3% to 14% above STC's. Both routes were unbiased. The restriction to STC was conservative rather than necessary. Both routes' multiply imputed intervals widened along the sweep more than the estimate's real spread (SE up to 0.28 against about 0.13), so coverage exceeded nominal.
findings: Refuting sentence holds: feasibility 0.998 to 1.000; MAIC SE / STC SE 1.03 to 1.14.
Effective sample size 85 to 231 of 300 along the sweep.
Bias at most 0.009 for both routes; coverage 0.956 to 1.000 (conservative toward the extremes).
QBA-13.not_answered: One binary unmeasured covariate, correct assumed relations, unanchored A side only, no decision reading. Peer review has not been done.
QBA-13.design: Unanchored transport with an unmeasured binary covariate imputed from its assumed relations; STC and MAIC sensitivity curves over the assumed target prevalence, with feasibility and effective sample size. 2 cells, 500 replicates each.
QBA-13.n_sim: 500 per scenario, 1,000 in total, each over a 5-point sweep with 10 imputations
QBA-13.estimand: A's marginal log odds in a target with the assumed prevalence of the unmeasured covariate

QBA-20.title: One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis of two bias layers reports robustness that the joint analysis does not support
QBA-20.question: Do one-at-a-time sensitivity analyses of population transportability and component invariance bound their joint effect on a cross-gap contrast, or can the layers offset and report spurious robustness?
QBA-20.answer: No. With an omitted modifier (population layer) and component drift (bridge layer) acting on one cross-gap log odds ratio of -0.20, each one-at-a-time curve stayed within 0.16 and never reversed the decision, while the joint elicited box reached a bias of -0.41 and 7% of it reversed the decision; 23% to 26% of the box lay outside the one-at-a-time envelope at every scale. Component-by-modifier drift, which current tooling excludes, moved the estimate by 0.04 alone because it acts through its product with the modifier imbalance.
findings: Scale 1: one-at-a-time envelope -0.156 to 0.157; joint -0.413 to 0.341; 7% of the box reverses the decision.
Masking: in 4% of the box both layers exceed 0.1 in absolute value and the net bias is below 0.05.
Elicited dependence: 32% to 34% of draws outside the one-at-a-time envelope when the layers are positively correlated, 21% to 24% independent, 5% to 12% negatively correlated.
QBA-20.not_answered: Population-level calculation on one logistic model; no sampling, component network fit or survival scale; joint covariate law known, so the cost of eliciting it is not measured; component non-additivity and backbone interactions not included. Peer review has not been done.
QBA-20.design: Population-level calculation on a logistic model: omitted-modifier imbalance, component main-effect drift and component-by-modifier drift varied one at a time and jointly over elicited ranges at three scales, with independent and dependent elicitations.
QBA-20.n_sim: Population-level calculation: 21^3 grid and 4000 elicited draws x 3 dependence structures at 3 scales
QBA-20.estimand: Bias of the reported target marginal log odds ratio of the cross-gap contrast
methods_compared: joint sensitivity region over both layers

QBA-23.title: Bootstrap intervals over a bias grid when resamples fail
QBA-23.question: When a bootstrap sensitivity analysis drops resamples whose weights fail near the edge of support, how does the interval behave, and is conditioning on success immaterial?
QBA-23.answer: No. Near the edge of the source's support, up to 67% of bootstrap resamples failed to produce MAIC weights, and the percentile interval from the survivors covered only 0.29 to 0.65 (0.14 to 0.56 counting failed original fits as giving no interval). The surviving resamples are those that contain the few patients who make the weights possible, so their spread understates the estimate's. The failure share should be reported as a result and the interval withheld where it is material.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: coverage given success 0.288 to 0.645 where more than 10% of resamples failed.
Where failures were rare, coverage 0.87 to 0.93, already below nominal at low effective sample size.
Effective sample size fell to about 3 of 100 or 5 of 300 at the most extreme assumed target mean.
QBA-23.not_answered: One covariate, continuous outcome; cost and surrogate approaches and identified sets not studied. Peer review has not been done.
QBA-23.design: Unanchored MAIC with a sweep of the assumed target mean toward the source's support boundary; percentile bootstrap intervals from successful resamples; coverage conditional on success and unconditional. 2 cells, 500 replicates each, 200 resamples.
QBA-23.n_sim: 500 per scenario, 1,000 in total, 200 resamples each at 4 grid points
QBA-23.estimand: A's target mean outcome at each assumed target covariate mean
methods_compared: MAIC with percentile bootstrap over successful resamples

QBA-24.title: Does a hazard-scale bias translate proportionally into RMST?
QBA-24.question: Can a sensitivity analysis stated as a hazard-ratio bias be reinterpreted as a proportional bias in RMST, the quantity the decision uses?
QBA-24.answer: No. The RMST change caused by a hazard-scale bias depends on the baseline hazard's shape and the event level: at the same survival by 24 months the same bias moved RMST up to 1.44 times as much for a decreasing as for an increasing hazard, and the proportional (first-order) reinterpretation understated the change by about 25% with few events and overstated it by up to 8% with many. A hazard-ratio sensitivity analysis must be translated with the baseline curve or stated on the RMST scale.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: ratio of largest to smallest RMST change across shapes 1.20 to 1.44 at matched survival.
Proportional prediction error at a bias hazard ratio of 2: -25% to -26% at 80% survival, -14% to -17% at 50%, -1% to +8% at 20%.
QBA-24.not_answered: Only the hazard-to-RMST translation; the PAIC layer, pseudo-IPD and curve-based arms, reconstruction error and tipping sets not run. Peer review has not been done.
QBA-24.design: Population-level numerical study: four baseline hazard shapes at three survival levels, bias hazard ratios 1.1 to 2, RMST at 24 months against the first-order proportional prediction.
QBA-24.n_sim: Population-level calculation: 4 shapes x 3 survival levels x 4 bias levels
QBA-24.estimand: Change in RMST at 24 months induced by a multiplicative hazard bias

QBA-25.title: Carrying a hazard-ratio bias into net benefit: the extrapolation family moved the decision more than the bias did
QBA-25.question: Does propagating a bias-corrected hazard ratio and its interval into an economic model reproduce the decision uncertainty, or does the bias need to share a parameter space with the extrapolation model?
QBA-25.answer: No. The probability of negative net benefit was 0.38 under point propagation of the reported hazard ratio and 0.67 when the bias (log hazard ratio within 0.15) and the treatment-effect extrapolation family were varied jointly. Almost all of the difference came from the extrapolation: a symmetric bias region alone moved the probability to 0.42, while a waning or cure extrapolation reversed the decision at the reported estimate. The worst joint combination (net benefit -9,618) was worse than any one-at-a-time scenario (-6,657).
findings: Reversal probability by family, joint over the bias: persisting 0.42, waning 0.82, cure 0.75.
Net benefit moved roughly linearly and symmetrically in the bias within each family, so a symmetric bias region barely changes the reversal probability.
Scenario analysis as currently recommended missed the joint worst case.
QBA-25.not_answered: Deterministic survival curves instead of fitted extrapolations; three families, no splines; one symmetric bias parameter; costs and utilities fixed; one price. Peer review has not been done.
QBA-25.design: Decision model with Weibull or cure control survival, a log hazard ratio bias elicited on [-0.15, 0.15], three treatment-effect extrapolation families; point propagation, scenario analysis and a joint probabilistic reference.
QBA-25.estimand: Probability of negative incremental net benefit (decision reversal)
methods_compared: joint probabilistic analysis over bias and extrapolation family

QBA-26.title: A single-covariate benchmark against omitted composite structure
QBA-26.question: Does the bias from dropping the strongest measured covariate bound the residual bias from several omitted variables, and does a scaled benchmark calibrate?
QBA-26.answer: No. With three or six omitted variables each no stronger than the strongest measured covariate, the leave-one-covariate-out benchmark covered the true residual bias in at most 7% of analyses, the bias being 1.4 to 5.7 times the benchmark. Scaling by the square root of the number of omitted variables did not fix it; scaling by the number itself did when each omitted variable was weaker than the strongest measured one. The benchmark also shrank as omitted structure grew, through odds-ratio non-collapsibility.
findings: Refuting sentence fails: plain benchmark coverage 0.00 to 0.07 for q of 3 or 6 with each omitted variable at most as strong as the strongest measured.
Scaled by sqrt(q): coverage 0.00 to 0.76; by the oracle correlation-adjusted factor: 0.00 to 0.98; by q: 0.99 to 1.00 at half strength and 0.57 to 0.67 at equal strength.
Median benchmark fell from 0.163 (one weak omitted variable) to 0.067 (six strong correlated ones) while the true bias rose from 0.08 to 0.56 and beyond.
QBA-26.not_answered: Omitted variables shifted in the same direction; one overlap level; negative-control route not run. Peer review has not been done.
QBA-26.design: Unanchored binary-outcome MAIC with four measured covariates and one, three or six correlated omitted covariates of varying strength; leave-one-covariate-out benchmark, unscaled and scaled by sqrt(q), by the oracle correlation-adjusted factor and by q; coverage of the true residual bias. 21 cells, 1000 replicates each.
QBA-26.estimand: A's marginal log odds in the target (the unanchored comparison's A side) and MAIC's residual bias
methods_compared: benchmark times the oracle correlation-adjusted factor

SFW-10.title: Stacking the weighting step into the MAIC sandwich makes intervals narrower, not better
SFW-10.question: Does a stacked sandwich that accounts for weight estimation give better MAIC intervals than the fixed-weight sandwich or the ESS-based conventional variance, and what population does a trimmed MAIC actually estimate?
SFW-10.answer: No. Stacking lowered the standard error in every untrimmed scenario (by up to 11%), because estimating calibration weights removes outcome variation the covariates explain; where MAIC intervals already undercover, at poor overlap, that made them worse (coverage down to 0.844). The fixed-weight sandwich was in band in 24 of 30 scenarios, the ESS-based variance in 18 and the stacked sandwich in 17, so current guidance stands. Trimming moved the estimand by up to 0.19 on the log odds ratio scale.
findings: Stacked over fixed-weight SE: 0.887 to 0.993, below 1 beyond Monte Carlo error in all 30 untrimmed scenarios; DESIGN.md's prediction of both signs fails.
Coverage: fixed-weight 0.893 to 0.960; ESS-based 0.885 to 0.980; stacked 0.844 to 0.953; stacked with n/(n-k) 0.847 to 0.953.
Every estimator loses coverage as ESS falls; the stacked sandwich fastest.
Trimming at the 95th percentile moved the estimand by up to 0.19; in 72% of trimmed scenarios the estimate was closer to the population the capped weights induce than to the declared target.
SFW-10.not_answered: No bootstrap and one sample size, so where stacking's asymptotic advantage appears is not located. Binary outcome, three covariates, MAIC on means. Peer review has not been done.
SFW-10.design: Binary-outcome MAIC with three covariates, 90 scenarios crossing target shift, event risk, effect modification and its alignment, and weight trimming; four variance estimators; trimmed analyses scored against the declared target and the induced population.
SFW-10.estimand: Target-population marginal log odds ratio, A versus C; for trimmed analyses also the effect in the population the capped weights induce

SFW-12.title: outstandR's G-computation estimate moved by about 0.05 on the log odds ratio across defensible target reconstructions
SFW-12.question: How much does outstandR's G-computation estimate depend on how it reconstructs the aggregate trial's covariate distribution from published means and SDs, when the true covariates are skewed and tail-dependent?
SFW-12.answer: Partly. Across five defensible reconstructions of the aggregate trial's covariates (normal or gamma margins; the IPD's, the target's, or no correlation), outstandR's G-computation estimate ranged by 0.049 to 0.052 on the log odds ratio scale within a dataset: at the registered materiality threshold, but about a fifth of its sampling SD. The default (normal margins, IPD correlation) was biased by -0.02 to -0.06 on skewed covariates; gamma margins removed most of it. Tail dependence in the true copula changed the range by at most 0.002.
findings: Margin family and correlation choice each contributed about half of the range.
Independence was the worst reconstruction; the IPD's correlation added bias when the target's differed.
Registered verdict: material, with the range at the threshold in every cell.
SFW-12.not_answered: Pairwise anchored comparison, two covariates, correct outcome model, point estimates only; no Bayesian G-computation, multiple-imputation marginalization or network use. Peer review has not been done.
SFW-12.design: Skewed target covariates with a Clayton or Gaussian copula, IPD with the same or a different correlation; outstandR's G-computation under five reconstructions (default, reported correlation, independence, gamma margins); anchored binary-outcome comparison. 4 cells, 400 replicates each.
SFW-12.estimand: Anchored marginal log odds ratio B versus A in the target
methods_compared: outstandR G-computation under five covariate reconstructions

SFW-14.title: drMAIC 0.1.0 returns the MAIC estimate as its doubly robust estimate, with an interval six times too narrow
SFW-14.question: Does drMAIC 0.1.0 implement a doubly robust MAIC with valid intervals: is its augmented estimate robust to a wrong weighting model when the outcome model is right, and do its intervals cover?
SFW-14.answer: No. drMAIC 0.1.0 averages the outcome model over the individual-data patients instead of the target population, so its doubly robust estimate equals its MAIC estimate in every replicate (difference below 2e-15) and keeps MAIC's bias when the weights are wrong and the outcome model right (0.066 against 0.004 for correct augmentation). Its analytic SE divides by n twice and mixes probability and log odds scales: 0.028 against an empirical SD of 0.17 to 0.22, coverage 0.20 to 0.26. Its percentile bootstrap covers 0.78 to 0.79.
findings: Defect 1: theta_stc = sum(w_norm * m_hat), so the augmented estimate reduces algebraically to the weighted mean of Y.
Defect 2 and 3: .dr_variance returns sum((w_norm*(Y-theta))^2)/n on the probability scale and it is reported as the SE of a log odds ratio.
Defect 4: bootstrap_ci() reweights on means only, refits the default outcome formula and holds the comparator fixed.
Wrong weights, right outcome model, target mean 0.5: drMAIC DR bias 0.066 (MCSE 0.007); correct augmentation 0.004; correct augmentation coverage 0.93 to 0.96 across cells.
SFW-14.not_answered: One package version, binary outcome, one sample size; G-MAIC not run; the time-to-event path (a weighted median labeled a hazard ratio) read from code, not simulated. Peer review has not been done.
SFW-14.design: Unanchored binary-outcome transport in a 2 x 2 of correct or wrong weighting and outcome models at two overlap levels; drMAIC's MAIC, DR estimate, analytic interval and bootstrap interval against a correctly augmented estimator. 8 cells, 600 replicates each, plus a bootstrap arm.
SFW-14.n_sim: 600 per cell, 8 cells; package bootstrap 150 per cell in 2 cells
SFW-14.estimand: Target-population marginal log odds ratio, A versus B
methods_compared: drMAIC doubly robust with analytic interval
correctly augmented weighting with bootstrap SE
